docs.title: Factor-Lake
docs.text:
Quantitative portfolio analysis and backtesting platform built on factor investing principles.

Factor-Lake lets you compose multi-factor stock selection models, run historical simulations against benchmark indices, and visualise performance through an interactive Streamlit UI backed by a Supabase cloud database.

docs.title: Backtests in AWS Lambda
docs.text: Backtests can run in AWS Lambda instead of inside the Streamlit app. The app sends only the inputs (factors, directions and sidebar settings). Lambda reads the market data from S3, runs the same backtest code, and saves the result in S3, so the app never has to download or hold the market data to run a backtest.

docs.title: 1. How it works
docs.text:
Streamlit app ──inputs──▶ Lambda factor-lake-backtest ──reads──▶ s3://.../factor-lake-data/*.parquet
      ▲                         │
      └──result or S3 link──────┴──saves──▶ s3://.../factor-lake-data/backtest-results/<hash>.json
  1. Inputs only. Run Portfolio Analysis (and Generate Comparison) sends a small JSON job: factors, directions, years, AUM, weighting, delisting strategy, factor combination, sectors and the fossil fuel filter. See src/backtest_jobs.py.
  2. Same code, same results. Lambda filters the data with src/universe_selection.py (the code behind Load Market Data) and runs src/backtest_engine.py, the code the app runs locally.
  3. Cached by hash. The result is saved under a SHA-256 hash of the inputs, the data version (the S3 ETags of the market data files) and the backtest code version (a hash of the engine's source files). Republishing the data or deploying new backtest code gives fresh results.
  4. Repeats are instant. When a result with that hash exists, Lambda returns it without rerunning the backtest. Results are shared, so a run by any user is cached for everyone.
  5. Result or link. Results up to 5 MB come back in the Lambda response (Lambda's limit is 6 MB). Bigger results come back as a temporary S3 link (valid for 1 hour), which the app downloads.
  6. 90-day expiry. An S3 lifecycle rule deletes saved results after 90 days.

The Results tab shows how each run was produced, for example "Computed: Returned from the AWS Lambda result cache in 0.4 s (first computed 2026-10-22 18:03:11 UTC)".

docs.title: 2. Deploy the Lambda
docs.text:
Needs AWS keys that can create IAM roles and Lambda functions, and change the bucket's lifecycle rules.

uv run python scripts/deploy_backtest_lambda.py

It is safe to run again: it creates what is missing and updates the rest. It sets up:

Resource Details IAM role factor-lake-backtest-lambda Read factor-lake-data/*, write factor-lake-data/backtest-results/*, CloudWatch logs Lambda factor-lake-backtest Python 3.12, 3008 MB, 10-minute timeout. pandas, numpy and pyarrow are bundled in the package at the versions your environment runs (Linux builds fetched with uv; unused parts such as test suites and pyarrow's Flight libraries removed), so Lambda computes with the same libraries as the app and needs no Lambda layer. The package (about 62 MB zipped, 199 MB unzipped; Lambda allows 250 MB) is uploaded to factor-lake-data/_deploy/ first, because direct uploads are limited to 50 MB S3 lifecycle rule factor-lake-expire-backtest-results Deletes factor-lake-data/backtest-results/ objects after 90 days. Other rules on the bucket are kept

Keys without IAM access (such as the class Sysen5900Student user, which is denied all IAM actions) cannot create the role. Deploy with an existing role instead: --role-arn <the role's ARN> (the script then makes no IAM calls). In the class account that is the course's Lambda role:

uv run python scripts/deploy_backtest_lambda.py --role-arn arn:aws:iam::620832638024:role/Sysen5900LambdaExecRole --function-name sysen5900-factor-lake-backtest

Without a usable role, run uv run python scripts/deploy_backtest_lambda.py --print-role-policy and send the output to an AWS admin. If the keys may not change the bucket's lifecycle rules, the deploy still finishes and says what to ask an admin for.

It finishes by pinging the function. Options: --memory, --timeout, --function-name, --role-arn, --package-only out.zip (build the zip without deploying).

docs.title: Deploy from CI
docs.text:
The app on Streamlit Cloud redeploys from main on every merge, and .github/workflows/deploy-lambda.yml keeps the Lambda in step with it. A push to main that changes src/, aws_lambda/, scripts/deploy_backtest_lambda.py or uv.lock (which sets the bundled pandas, numpy and pyarrow versions) runs:

  1. Unit tests. The workflow calls tests.yml. Nothing is deployed unless the tests pass.
  2. Deploy. It runs uv sync --locked, then the deploy command above with --role-arn and --function-name from the repository variables, plus --leave-lifecycle-rules, so CI never rewrites the shared bucket's lifecycle settings (it only checks them; the 90-day rule is an admin's, section 9). The Python version comes from .python-version, so the Lambda gets the library versions locked in uv.lock. The WRDS data folder is the code's default (DEFAULT_WRDS_DIR in src/wrds_data.py), so a new WRDS pull is one code change.
  3. Check. It runs scripts/check_backtest_lambda.py (section 4) against the new function: the Legacy samples, then one quarterly WRDS backtest end to end.

The run fails if any step fails, so a red run means the Lambda may be behind main. To redeploy by hand, open Actions → Deploy Backtest Lambda → Run workflow (only main deploys). Deploys never overlap. A push that arrives during a deploy waits for it to finish.

A repository admin has to add these under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions:

Kind Name Value Secret AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY Keys that may update the function, pass its role, upload to factor-lake-data/_deploy/ and read the market data (the class Sysen5900Student keys can) Variable LAMBDA_ROLE_ARN arn:aws:iam::620832638024:role/Sysen5900LambdaExecRole Variable LAMBDA_FUNCTION_NAME sysen5900-factor-lake-backtest

Until all four are set, the workflow stops at its first step and names what is missing. It never falls back to the script's default function name.

Old packages are not deleted. Each package in factor-lake-data/_deploy/ is named by its content hash, so a deploy with unchanged code reuses the same file, and only real changes add a new one (about 62 MB each). To clear them out, delete all but the newest few backtest-lambda-*.zip files in the S3 console, or ask an AWS admin for a lifecycle rule on factor-lake-data/_deploy/.

docs.title: 3. Turn it on in the app
docs.text:
Set the function name next to the AWS keys, in .env locally or in the Streamlit Cloud secrets:

FACTOR_LAKE_BACKTEST_LAMBDA="factor-lake-backtest"

The app's AWS key also needs lambda:InvokeFunction on that function. When the variable is set, the sidebar shows Run backtests in AWS Lambda (on by default). Turn it off to run backtests in the app as before (Load Market Data first). Without the variable, the app works exactly as before.

docs.title: 4. Check it
docs.text:
uv run python scripts/check_backtest_lambda.py

For four sample backtests (Mixing and Integrating, every delisting strategy, equal and market cap weighting, the fossil fuel filter and a cohort comparison), it runs each one locally on the S3 data, then in Lambda, and compares every number. It then runs each one in Lambda again and checks that it came from the cache, unchanged. It uses new inputs each time, so the first Lambda call always computes. The Lambda uses the same library versions but runs on Linux x86, so numbers may differ in the last binary digit. The check allows a relative difference of 1e-9 and prints the largest difference it found.

Then it checks one quarterly WRDS backtest (2008-2026, two factors) end to end. The function must read the WRDS folder the code expects (its FACTOR_LAKE_WRDS_DIR). The Lambda's result must match the same job run locally on the WRDS data in S3. The newest rebalance date's holdings, read from the Lambda's holdings file the way the app reads them (two ranged GETs), must match the local holdings of that date. A second Lambda call must come from the cache, unchanged. --skip-wrds leaves this part out.

Holdings are compared stock by stock, leaving out Rank and Score. Winsorizing gives the top 1% of each factor exactly the same score, and the engine sorts those ties in an order that depends on the machine. So a Mac and Lambda can list tied stocks in a different order, and for a stock bought by several Mixing sleeves, show the Rank and Score from a different sleeve. The stocks held, shares, prices, weights, returns and contributions still have to match. When a percentage cuts through a tied block (for example a 1% cohort), the engine's choice of which tied stocks to buy also depends on the machine and on row order. That is a known engine issue, to be fixed separately with deterministic tie-breaking.

The unit tests (tests/unit/test_backtest_lambda.py) run the same Lambda code against a fake S3 and drive the real app, checking that a Lambda run equals a local run for both factor combinations, each delisting strategy and the cohort comparison, and that a repeated run is served from the cache.

docs.title: 5. Demo script (about 5 minutes)
docs.text:
Before the call: deploy (section 2), add FACTOR_LAKE_BACKTEST_LAMBDA to .env, and start the app with uv run streamlit run app/streamlit_app.py. To warm the Lambda up, run one backtest. To keep the "first run computes" moment for the call, pick inputs you have not run yet (for example a new AUM).

  1. The switch. Point out Run backtests in AWS Lambda in the sidebar and the caption with the function name. On the Analysis tab, the caption says the market data does not need to be loaded.
  2. First run computes in Lambda. Add two factors (for example ROE using 9/30 Data and ROA %), pick Integrating, and click Run Portfolio Analysis without loading data. The confirmation says "computed in AWS Lambda in N s". In the Results tab, the Computed line shows the result ID (the first 12 characters of its hash).
  3. The repeat is cached. Click Run Portfolio Analysis again with the same settings. The new run shows the same result ID and "returned from the AWS Lambda result cache in 0.N s", with the time it was first computed.
  4. Any change is a new backtest. Change the AUM or a factor direction and run again: it computes (new result ID).
  5. Same results as before. Turn the Lambda switch off, click Load Market Data, and run the same settings as step 2. The new run tab shows the same final value, CAGR and holdings as the Lambda run. For the precise check, run scripts/check_backtest_lambda.py in a terminal: "match: yes" with the largest difference for each backtest, and "cached=True" for every repeat.
  6. Cohort comparison. In a Lambda run's tab, open Run Cohort Comparison and click Generate Comparison: the caption says it ran in Lambda.
  7. Where results live. In the AWS console: S3 → sysen-5900-factor-lake → factor-lake-data/backtest-results/ shows one JSON file per result hash. Management → Lifecycle rules shows the 90-day expiry (in the class account an admin has to add it; see section 2). Lambda → factor-lake-backtest (sysen5900-factor-lake-backtest in the class account) → Monitor shows the invocations, and its CloudWatch logs show "Computed ..." and "Cache hit ..." lines.

docs.title: 6. Share an analysis by its ID
docs.text:
The hash a result is saved under doubles as its analysis ID. Each saved file holds the job (factors, directions, settings) next to the result, so the ID alone is enough to show the analysis again. The app reads it straight from S3 (src/saved_analyses.py), without calling the Lambda, so opening never reruns a backtest.

  • Each Lambda run's tab shows the full ID with a copy button.
  • Results → Open a saved analysis opens an ID as a new tab with the original results and settings.
  • This session's analyses lists only the runs of the current browser session. Nothing is listed from S3, so nobody sees other people's analyses unless they're given an ID.
  • Earlier analyses on this browser (app/analysis_history.py) lists IDs from earlier sessions on the same browser. The app has no logins, so they are kept in the browser's localStorage (key factor-lake-analyses, newest 200). A small inline JavaScript component (st.components.v2) adds each session's IDs and reports the stored list to the app once per page load. Reporting more often would rerun the app and clear messages like "Analysis complete".
  • All saved analyses lists everyone's newest 20 from S3 (list_saved_analyses). It reads only the files' metadata (the Lambda saves a short summary and the kind, so cohort comparisons and WRDS ranked lists are left out), and only while expanded. Only <ID>.json results are listed, never the WRDS holdings files next to them. A WRDS analysis's summary starts with its data source and frequency, e.g. "WRDS, Quarterly | ROE (higher), ROA (higher) | Mixing | 2008-2026 | $1,000", and the session and browser lists show the same line under a WRDS run's label. The app's key needs s3:ListBucket on backtest-results/; without it the list explains that. Results saved before summaries existed show "Details not recorded".
  • Errors: text that isn't a 64-character ID, an ID with no saved analysis (mistyped, or deleted by the 90-day rule), a result saved before sharing existed, or a cohort comparison's ID.

Demo (about 2 minutes, after the steps in section 5):

  1. In a run's tab, copy its Analysis ID.
  2. Open the app in a second browser window (a private window works) to stand in for a colleague. Its Results tab shows Open a saved analysis and no runs.
  3. Paste the ID and click Open analysis. The same final value, CAGR, holdings and charts appear in a tab labelled "(opened)", with "Opened from a saved analysis (first computed …)". Generate Comparison also works there.
  4. Paste a wrong ID (for example drop the last character, or change one character) to show the errors: "is not an analysis ID" and "No saved analysis has the ID … deleted after 90 days".
  5. Back in the first window, This session's analyses lists your runs with their IDs. The second window lists only the analysis it opened.
  6. Close both windows, open the app again in the first browser, and go to Results → Earlier analyses on this browser: the analyses from before are listed with their IDs. Click Open on one, and it opens without pasting anything.
  7. Expand All saved analyses to show everyone's recent analyses with their factors and dates, and open one from there.

docs.title: 7. Troubleshoot
docs.text: Message Fix Could not call the backtest Lambda ... AccessDeniedException The app's AWS key needs lambda:InvokeFunction on the function ... ResourceNotFoundException Deploy the function (section 2) or fix FACTOR_LAKE_BACKTEST_LAMBDA The backtest Lambda failed: Task timed out Raise --timeout (up to 900 seconds) and redeploy ... Runtime.OutOfMemory Raise --memory and redeploy The backtest Lambda could not run this backtest: ... The backtest itself failed; the message is the engine's error

docs.title: 8. Cost
docs.text: Each uncached backtest is one Lambda invocation of a few seconds. A cold start adds the time to download the 8 MB market data file. Cached repeats take well under a second, and saved results are small JSON files deleted after 90 days. Class use stays far inside the Lambda and S3 free tiers.

docs.title: 9. WRDS mode
docs.text:
WRDS backtests (see the user guide, section 15, and DOCS/WRDS_MODE_DESIGN.md) run in the same function. A job with data_mode: "wrds" goes to src/wrds_service.py; every other job is a Legacy job, handled exactly as before.

  • Data. The function reads three files under factor-lake-data/wrds_2026_10/ (factor_panel_monthly, returns_monthly, market_monthly), only the columns it needs, once per container. The folder is set by the function's FACTOR_LAKE_WRDS_DIR variable (the deploy script's --wrds-dir). A new WRDS pull goes into a new folder.
  • Cache. The key hashes the job, the S3 ETags of the three files and a WRDS code version. Legacy keeps its own code version, so WRDS changes never recompute Legacy results.
  • Holdings. A WRDS backtest writes backtest-results/<hash>.holdings.parquet (one row group per rebalance date) before backtest-results/<hash>.json. The app reads one date at a time with its own S3 keys, in two ranged GETs. A cached result whose holdings file is missing is computed again.
  • Listings. The result JSON's metadata has the job's kind and a summary starting "WRDS, " (section 6). WRDS results saved before this (on the dev function) have none and show "Details not recorded" until the 90-day rule deletes them.
  • Live deploys come from CI (section 2, "Deploy from CI"), whose check step runs a WRDS backtest end to end.

docs.title: Deploy a dev function
docs.text:
Test changes on a separate function and leave the live one alone:

uv run python scripts/deploy_backtest_lambda.py --function-name sysen5900-factor-lake-backtest-dev \
    --role-arn <the course role's ARN> --leave-lifecycle-rules
  • --leave-lifecycle-rules does not write the bucket's lifecycle rules (a normal deploy rewrites them, and the bucket is shared with the live app). It only reads them and says whether backtest-results/ expires.
  • --wrds-dir wrds_YYYY_MM points the function at another WRDS folder (default wrds_2026_10).

To point a local app at the dev function, set the function name next to the AWS keys in .streamlit/secrets.toml (top level):

FACTOR_LAKE_BACKTEST_LAMBDA = "sysen5900-factor-lake-backtest-dev"

To check the WRDS engine locally on the pipeline's files (IWM tracking, run time and memory), run uv run python scripts/check_wrds_engine.py "<path>/processed/final". It prints its results and stores none.

docs.title: Validation on the dev function (2026-10-28)
docs.text:
Lambda's own durations (from the invocation log tail), 3008 MB function, course role. All runs were computed (no cache) unless marked.

Job Container Duration Max memory Result JSON Holdings Parquet Result Monthly, whole universe, cap weighted (IWM tracking check) cold: init 2.5 s, plus loading the WRDS data 10.2 s 1154 MB 85 KB 47.9 MB PASS (correlation ≥ 0.99, tracking error ≤ 3%) Monthly, Mixing, 3 factors warm 3.0 s 1154 MB 85 KB 22.1 MB Monthly, Integrating, 2 factors warm 1.5 s 1154 MB 85 KB 6.0 MB Monthly, Mixing, 3 factors, cap weighted warm 2.9 s 1154 MB 85 KB 23.3 MB Monthly, Mixing, 4 factors warm 3.5 s 1154 MB 85 KB 27.6 MB Monthly, Mixing, 10 factors warm 6.5 s 1154 MB 85 KB 49.7 MB The first one again warm, cache hit 0.11 s 1154 MB 85 KB 3 jobs at once: semi-annual / quarterly / monthly 1 warm, 2 cold (init 2.6 s) 0.5 / 6.9 / 8.6 s 1154 / 890 / 996 MB 16 / 29 / 84 KB 2.3 / 5.1 / 16.8 MB all finished, 9.6 s wall From the app: semi-annual / quarterly / monthly backtest warm 0.7 / 1.1 / 2.9 s 996 MB 16 / 30 / 85 KB 3.3 / 7.0 / 22.1 MB PASS From the app: cohort comparison (monthly, 10%) warm 3.6 s 996 MB 11 KB PASS From the app: ranked list, one date warm 0.3 s 996 MB 0.9 MB PASS From the app: Legacy backtest warm 2.4 s 996 MB 2.3 MB equals main's result (≤ 1e-9 relative)
  • Warm repeats do not slow down on Linux. Five different monthly jobs in a row on one container took time in line with their number of factors, not their order. (On Windows, repeated engine runs in one process did get slower.)
  • Cold start for WRDS: about 2.5 s of Lambda init, plus a few seconds the first WRDS job of a container spends loading the WRDS data.
  • Memory: at most about 1.15 GB of the function's 3008 MB, with the Legacy and WRDS data both loaded.
  • Package: 61.7 MB zipped, 199 MB unzipped (Lambda allows 250 MB).

docs.title: Admin: confirm the 90-day rule
docs.text: Saved results and WRDS holdings both live under factor-lake-data/backtest-results/, so one lifecycle rule on that prefix expires both. The class keys cannot read the bucket's lifecycle rules, so an AWS admin must confirm that the rule factor-lake-expire-backtest-results (prefix factor-lake-data/backtest-results/, expire after 90 days) is enabled on sysen-5900-factor-lake.

docs.title: AWS S3 Data Source
docs.text: Use this guide when you need to configure, update, or troubleshoot where the Factor-Lake app loads its market data from.

docs.title: Latest WRDS data
docs.text:
The newest data version is s3://sysen-5900-factor-lake/factor-lake-data/wrds_2026_10/ (data version 2026-10-25), built by the WRDS pipeline in pipeline/ from the October 2026 WRDS, Fama-French and FRED pulls. Every column is described in pipeline/DATA_DICTIONARY.md.

key under wrds_2026_10/ contents factor_panel_monthly.parquet point-in-time factor panel: every Russell 2000 member (IWM holding) at each month end, with fundamental, price and analyst factors, betas and next-month return universe_periods.parquet each stock's Russell 2000 membership periods returns_monthly.parquet monthly returns of every stock ever in the index, delisting returns included prices_daily/year=YYYY/data.parquet daily CRSP prices, returns, shares and market cap, one file per year prices_daily/_manifest.json the years, rows and columns of the daily files (uploaded last) market_daily.parquet, market_monthly.parquet Russell 2000 index and ETF returns, Fama-French factors, Treasury and Moody's yields rv_multiples_monthly.parquet valuation multiples with their GICS industry and sector percentile ranks rv_peer_stats_monthly.parquet peer percentiles of every multiple by GICS industry and month dcf_inputs_annual.parquet annual statements and FCFF for DCF valuation estimates_consensus.parquet the full IBES consensus (7 measures, FY1-FY3 and long-term growth), linked to permno fundamentals_quarterly.parquet quarterly Compustat statements, TTM sums and quarter-end factors security_master.parquet ids, names and GICS classification of every stock column_stats.parquet statistics of every column of the other files

Where each source ends: CRSP prices 2026-09-30, IWM holdings 2026-06-30, Compustat 2026-09-30, IBES 2026-08-20, Fama-French 2026-08-31, FRED 2026-10-22.

The live app still reads the older files (full_precision_test.parquet, last_price_mapping.parquet, daily_prices/) until the "switch app to new data" story moves it to this folder. Each new data pull gets its own wrds_YYYY_MM/ folder, and this section is updated to point at it. How the folder is built, uploaded and inspected: pipeline/README.md; the S3 setup: DOCS/AWS_S3_DATA.md.

docs.title: 1. Know the setup
docs.text:
1. The Streamlit app still runs on Streamlit Community Cloud.
  2. The market data lives in AWS S3 as two Parquet files, not in a database.
  3. S3 is always on. It does not pause after a week without traffic the way the free-tier Supabase project did.
  4. The app downloads the data once per server process (about 1–2 seconds) and shares that copy with every user session for 6 hours.
  5. Supabase is still supported as a fallback data source.
File Former Supabase table Contents s3://sysen-5900-factor-lake/factor-lake-data/full_precision_test.parquet Full Precision Test Yearly factor data for the investment universe s3://sysen-5900-factor-lake/factor-lake-data/last_price_mapping.parquet last_price_mapping Delisting dates and last prices

Every publish also keeps a copy under factor-lake-data/archive/<UTC timestamp>/ for rollback.

docs.title: 2. Configure the app
docs.text:
Add these to the Streamlit Cloud app's Secrets (or .streamlit/secrets.toml / .env locally):

AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID = "your-access-key-id"
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = "your-secret-access-key"
AWS_DEFAULT_REGION = "us-east-1"
  1. With AWS credentials present, the app uses S3 automatically. The sidebar's Data Source line shows "AWS S3 (Parquet files)".
  2. Set FACTOR_LAKE_DATA_SOURCE = "supabase" to switch back to Supabase without a code change, or "s3" to force S3.
  3. Optional: FACTOR_LAKE_S3_BUCKET (default sysen-5900-factor-lake) and FACTOR_LAKE_S3_PREFIX (default factor-lake-data) point the app at other files.
  4. The app only needs read access. Ask the AWS account owner for a key whose policy allows just s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::sysen-5900-factor-lake/factor-lake-data/*, rather than reusing a key that can write or delete.
  5. Never commit keys. .env and .streamlit/secrets.toml are in .gitignore.

docs.title: 3. Publish new data
docs.text:
Use scripts/publish_data_to_s3.py with a key that can write to the bucket.

  1. Put AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in .env.
  2. Check the files first without uploading:
uv run python scripts/publish_data_to_s3.py --universe new_data.xlsx --delisting last_price_mapping.csv --dry-run
  1. Publish:
uv run python scripts/publish_data_to_s3.py --universe new_data.xlsx --delisting last_price_mapping.csv
  1. Files can be .csv, .xlsx, .xls or .parquet, with the same columns as the former Supabase tables.
  2. The script refuses files the app could not use (for example, no Date column), uploads, and reads the file back to confirm the row count.
  3. The app picks up the new data within 6 hours. To see it immediately, reboot the app from Streamlit Cloud (Manage app → Reboot app).
  4. To copy the current Supabase tables instead, use --from-supabase (needs SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_KEY).

docs.title: 4. Publish the daily stock data
docs.text:
The daily CRSP prices for the Russell 2000 universe (russell2000_cleaned.csv, about 7.5 million rows) are published separately with scripts/publish_daily_data_to_s3.py. The app does not use them yet.

  1. Put AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (a key that can write to the bucket) in .env.
  2. Check the file first. This cleans it and writes the Parquet files locally without uploading:
uv run python scripts/publish_daily_data_to_s3.py path/to/russell2000_cleaned.csv --dry-run --output-dir daily_parquet
  1. Publish:
uv run python scripts/publish_daily_data_to_s3.py path/to/russell2000_cleaned.csv

Add --start-date 2010-01-01 to drop earlier rows. The data published on 2026-10-15 used this option: 6.57M rows, 5,117 securities, 2010-01-04 to 2024-12-31. 4. It first checks that the AWS keys can write to the bucket (a few seconds), so a wrong key fails right away with a readable message. Expect about 1 minute and under 1 GB of memory for 7.5 million rows.

The cleaning matches the old daily loader and the yearly data:

  • Column names can be upper or lower case: date, permno, ticker, prc, cfacpr, shrout, ret, vol. Other columns are not published, and the script lists them.
  • Placeholders such as --, CRSP letter codes, and CRSP's numeric missing codes become missing values. That covers returns below -100% (-66, -77, -88, -99), negative volume, and shares outstanding of 0.
  • Rows without a date, a price or an identifier are dropped. A price of 0 counts as missing.
  • prc is made positive, because CRSP marks bid/ask midpoints with a negative price.
  • prc_adj = prc / cfacpr (split-adjusted).
  • mkt_cap = prc × shrout, in $ thousands.
  • For duplicate permno/date rows, the first one is kept. If the file has no permno column, only exact copies are dropped, because share classes can share a ticker. The script reports how many ticker/date pairs still have more than one row.

What ends up in S3:

File Contents factor-lake-data/daily_prices/year=YYYY/data.parquet One file per year, sorted by security and date factor-lake-data/daily_last_prices.parquet Each security's last trading day and price. ended_early is set when its rows stop more than 7 days before the data ends. That is a delisting, or leaving the universe if the file only covers Russell 2000 membership periods factor-lake-data/daily_prices/_manifest.json Years, row counts, columns and the cleaning summary. Uploaded last, so readers never see a half-published set

Read it in Python with S3DataManager().read_daily_prices(years=[2020, 2021]). Leave out years to load everything.

Re-publishing replaces the yearly files in place and uploads the manifest last. If a re-publish is interrupted, run it again before using the data.

docs.title: 5. Roll back a bad publish
docs.text:
1. Find the previous good copy under factor-lake-data/archive/ in the S3 console.
  2. Download its two files and publish them again with step 3.

docs.title: 6. Check the app under load
docs.text:
scripts/load_test_sessions.py opens 5 browser sessions at the same time, and each runs a full backtest: Load Market Data, Run Portfolio Analysis, Results, and the cohort comparison.

  1. Run it against the live app from the Actions tab (Load Test → Run workflow, .github/workflows/load-test.yml). It only runs when someone starts it. A failed run means at least one session failed; screenshots are attached to the run.
  2. Or run it locally:
pip install playwright && playwright install chromium
python scripts/load_test_sessions.py --url http://localhost:8501 --rounds 3

docs.title: 7. Troubleshoot
docs.text:
1. "AWS credentials are not configured": add AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY to the app's secrets.
  2. "Could not read s3://... (AccessDenied)": the key cannot read that file. Check its IAM policy.
  3. "Could not read s3://... (NoSuchKey)": the file was not published, or the bucket or prefix setting is wrong.
  4. After fixing secrets, reboot the app so the new values load.

docs.title: 8. Cost
docs.text:
At standard S3 prices (us-east-1), costs are well under $1 per month, far inside the $50 per month budget:

  • Storage is about $0.023 per GB-month. The yearly data is about 8 MB per publish and the daily data about 300 MB.
  • Downloads cost about $0.0004 per 1,000 requests.
  • Data transfer out stays within the AWS free tier at this volume.

docs.title: General Approach
docs.text: The Factor Lake team has agreed to take a SecDevOps approach to our project's development and all contributors are expected to do the same. SecDevOps is a software development approach that prioritizes security.^1 All contributors must abide by Factor Lake's Secure Coding Standard.

docs.title: Static Analysis Using Bandit
docs.text:
Static analysis techniques are used to evaluate a source code's formatting consistency, adherence to coding standards, documentation conventions, and security vulnerabilities without executing it. Per Snyk.io, "static code analysis will enable us to detect code bugs or vulnerabilities that other testing methods and tools, such as manual code reviews and compilers, frequently miss." ^2

Static Application Security Testing (SAST) is a subset of static analysis testing that our team has decided to focus on. SAST prioritizes the detection of security vulnerabilities as opposed to things like code style deviations and optimization issues. SAST tools are "designed specifically to find security issues with high accuracy, striving for low false positive and false negative rates, and providing detailed information about root causes and remedies of spotted vulnerabilities."^3

The first tool we've decided to use for SAST is Bandit. Per their documentation, "Bandit is a tool designed to find common security issues in Python code. To do this, Bandit processes each file, builds an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) from it, and runs appropriate plugins against the AST nodes. Once Bandit has finished scanning all the files, it generates a report."^4

The second tool we've decided to use for SAST is Safety CLI. Per their documentation, "Safety CLI is a Python dependency vulnerability scanner designed to enhance software supply chain security and enable the secure use of Python packages."^5 The project's dependencies are managed in pyproject.toml and pinned via uv.lock.

docs.title: Documentation Contributor Guide
docs.text: This guide is for team members who want to add or edit documentation on the Factor-Lake docs site.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The docs site is built with MkDocs and publishes automatically to GitHub Pages when you push to main in the Factor-Lake GitHub Repo. To add or edit documentation, follow this sequence:

  1. Edit or create a markdown file in DOCS/.
  2. Register the page in mkdocs.yml.
  3. Add a quick link in DOCS/index.md.
  4. Preview locally if needed.
  5. Push to main and let GitHub Actions deploy the site.

docs.title: Project links
docs.text: Tool Link GitHub Repo Factor-Lake GitHub Repo Streamlit App Factor-Lake Streamlit App Supabase Project Factor Lake Supabase Project Trello Board Quant Finance Project Trello ScrumPoker ScrumPoker Online Streamlit Cloud Streamlit Cloud

docs.title: Step 1: Create or edit your markdown file
For a new guide
docs.text:
1. Create a new .md file in the DOCS/ folder.
  2. Example: DOCS/MY_NEW_GUIDE.md
  3. Use a descriptive filename with no spaces.
  4. Start the file with a top-level heading.
  5. Write the guide as a step-by-step procedure with short sections.

Example:

# My New Guide Title

1. Do the first thing.
2. Do the next thing.
3. Verify the result.

docs.title: For an existing guide
docs.text:
1. Open the .md file in DOCS/.
  2. Rewrite the content so a new team member can follow it without guessing.
  3. Replace plain-text tool names with embedded links where possible.
  4. Save the file.

docs.title: Step 2: Update mkdocs.yml
docs.text:
The mkdocs.yml file at the repo root controls site navigation.

  1. Open mkdocs.yml.
  2. Find the nav: section.
  3. Add your guide under Guides in the same style as the existing entries.
  4. Make sure the display name and filename are correct and case-sensitive.

Example:

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - Guides:
    - Factor Lake User Guide: FACTOR_LAKE_USER_GUIDE.md
    - Developer Onboarding: DEV_ONBOARDING.md
    - New Guide Name: NEW_GUIDE.md

docs.title: Step 3: Update DOCS/index.md
docs.text:
The home page of the docs site has a quick-links table.

  1. Open DOCS/index.md.
  2. Find the quick-links table.
  3. Add a row for the new guide.
  4. Keep the link text and file name consistent with mkdocs.yml.

Example:

| [New Guide Name](NEW_GUIDE.md) | Short description of what the guide covers |

docs.title: Step 4: Preview locally
docs.text:
1. Install MkDocs if you have not already:
uv sync --group docs
  1. From the repo root, run:
uv run mkdocs serve
  1. Open the local site at http://127.0.0.1:8000/.
  2. Verify the new page appears in the navigation and renders correctly.
  3. Check that links, tables, and code blocks display as expected.

docs.title: Step 5: Commit and push
docs.text:
1. Stage the changed files.
  2. Commit with a clear message.
  3. Push to main.

Example:

git add DOCS/MY_NEW_GUIDE.md mkdocs.yml DOCS/index.md
git commit -m "Add documentation guide"
git push origin main

docs.title: Step 6: Verify deployment
docs.text:
1. Open the Factor-Lake GitHub Repo.
  2. Check the Actions tab.
  3. Confirm the workflow named Deploy MkDocs to GitHub Pages passed.
  4. Open the published docs site and confirm the new page appears.

docs.title: The page does not appear in the menu
docs.text:
1. Check the filename in mkdocs.yml.
  2. Make sure the file exists in DOCS/.
  3. Confirm the indentation in mkdocs.yml is correct.

docs.title: The quick link is broken
docs.text:
1. Check the file path in DOCS/index.md.
  2. Use the filename only, not DOCS/filename.md.
  3. Make sure the link text and filename match the nav entry.

docs.title: Tables or code blocks render incorrectly
docs.text:
1. Check Markdown syntax carefully.
  2. Verify table pipes and code fences are balanced.
  3. Re-run mkdocs serve and confirm the page builds cleanly.

docs.title: The workflow fails
docs.text:
1. Open the failing GitHub Actions run.
  2. Read the build log for YAML or dependency errors.
  3. Fix the file locally and push again.

docs.title: Factor Lake User Workflow
docs.text: Use this guide when you want to run a factor experiment in the Factor-Lake Streamlit App and turn it into a class result.

docs.title: 1. Open the project links
docs.text: Tool Link Streamlit App Factor-Lake Streamlit App

docs.title: 2. Understand the app in one sentence
docs.text: Factor Lake lets you choose a group of stock-selection factors, rank stocks by those factors, run a historical backtest, and compare the result to benchmarks.

docs.title: 3. Start each analysis with the same order
docs.text:
1. Open the Streamlit app.
  2. Set sidebar controls.
  3. Choose factors.
  4. Load data.
  5. Run the backtest.
  6. Read the results.

docs.title: 4. Set the sidebar first
docs.text:
The steps below are for the default Legacy data source. For WRDS data with semi-annual, quarterly or monthly rebalancing, see 15. Use WRDS mode.

  1. Decide whether to restrict fossil fuel companies.
  2. Choose equal weight or market cap weight.
  3. Choose how multiple factors are combined:
  4. Mixing (default): each factor buys its own top stocks with an equal share of the money. A stock picked by two factors is held twice.
  5. Integrating: stocks are ranked by their average score across all the factors and the top ones are bought once each. Stocks missing any selected factor are left out. With one factor, both give the same portfolio.
  6. Turn on sector filtering only if you need it.
  7. Set the start and end years.
  8. Set the initial investment amount.
  9. Pick the delisting strategy you want to test.

docs.title: 5. Choose factors and directions
docs.text:
1. Open the Analysis tab.
  2. Select one or more factors.
  3. Decide whether each selected factor should rank high-to-low or low-to-high.
  4. Keep the direction consistent with the financial meaning of the factor.
  5. If you are unsure, start with one factor and add more later.

docs.title: 6. Load the market data
docs.text:
1. Click Load Market Data.
  2. Wait for the app to fetch data.
  3. Confirm the filters you chose are applied.
  4. Make sure the app says the data loaded successfully.

docs.title: 7. Run the backtest
docs.text:
1. Click Run Portfolio Analysis.
  2. Wait for the simulation to complete.
  3. Confirm you see a success message. It names the saved run, e.g. "Run 2: ROA %".
  4. Open the Results tab. The newest run's tab is selected automatically.

docs.title: Saved runs
docs.text:
1. Every successful run is saved as its own tab in Results, newest first.
  2. The captions at the top of each tab show the factors and directions, period, initial AUM, universe, factor combination method, weighting, and delisting strategy that run used.
  3. Saved tabs do not change when you edit the sidebar or factors afterwards. Run the analysis again to create a new tab.
  4. Click Remove this run to delete a tab you no longer need.
  5. Only the last 5 runs are kept, and all saved runs are cleared when you refresh the page, so record your numbers.

docs.title: Share an analysis or open it later
docs.text:
When backtests run in AWS Lambda, every analysis is saved for 90 days under an analysis ID.

  1. The ID is shown in the captions at the top of each run's tab. Click the copy button on the right of the ID.
  2. To open an analysis (yours or a colleague's), go to Results → Open a saved analysis, paste the ID and click Open analysis. It opens as a new tab, labelled "(opened)", with the original results, factors and settings. It loads from S3 and does not rerun the backtest.
  3. This session's analyses in the Results tab lists every analysis you ran or opened since the page was loaded, with its ID, including runs no longer shown as tabs. It never shows other people's analyses.
  4. Forgot to copy an ID? Earlier analyses on this browser lists the analyses you ran or opened in earlier sessions on the same browser, each with its ID and an Open button. They are kept in your browser only, so they don't follow you to another computer and disappear if you clear the site's data.
  5. All saved analyses lists everyone's saved analyses (newest 20), with their factors, method, period and starting amount, and an Open button. It loads only when you expand it. WRDS analyses start with "WRDS" and their frequency, e.g. "WRDS, Quarterly | ROE (higher), ROA (higher) | ...", and the two lists above show the same line under a WRDS run.
  6. Runs computed in the app (with the Lambda switch off) are not saved, so they have no ID.
  7. An ID that is mistyped, or older than 90 days, shows an error saying no saved analysis has that ID.

docs.title: 8. Read the results in order
docs.text:
1. Pick the run tab you want and check its captions.
  2. Start with Performance Summary.
  3. Check the Holdings and Ranks table. Pick a rebalance year to see every stock the backtest bought that year: its rank, score, factor values, weight, shares, buy price, dollar value, period return, contribution and whether it was delisted. Mixing runs also show which factors picked each stock. The contributions add up to the portfolio return shown above the table. Download CSV exports the full table.
  4. Review Portfolio Growth Over Time.
  5. Review Year-by-Year Performance.
  6. Review Top vs Bottom Cohort Analysis. It uses the settings of the run tab it is in.
  7. Review Advanced Backtest Statistics.
  8. Review Yearly Win/Loss Summary.

docs.title: Check the raw data
docs.text:
1. Open the Data Viewer tab after loading market data in the Analysis tab. It uses that data and downloads nothing new.
  2. Pick a date range, and optionally one or more sectors or industries. Leaving a list empty means all of them.
  3. Click Load data to see the matching rows, then Download CSV to save exactly that table.
  4. Changing a filter or clicking Clear removes the table. Click Load data again to see it.

docs.title: 9. Keep the factor logic straight
docs.text:
1. ROE and ROA are profitability signals.
  2. Momentum signals look for continuation in price performance.
  3. Price-to-book and earnings yield are valuation signals.
  4. Volatility and accruals are quality/risk proxies.
  5. Asset growth and CapEx growth are growth signals.

docs.title: 10. Know what the app is measuring
docs.text:
1. Returns come from the Next-Year Return % field.
  2. Delisting handling depends on the strategy you choose.
  3. The backtest is historical, not predictive.
  4. One strong result is not enough on its own.

docs.title: 11. Avoid the common mistakes
docs.text:
1. Do not run the backtest before loading data.
  2. Changing settings does not update saved tabs. Run again to create a new tab. If you change sectors, the fossil-fuel filter, or years, click Load Market Data first.
  3. Do not compare experiments with different time windows without noting it.
  4. Do not assume one factor is always best.

docs.title: 12. Troubleshoot when results look wrong
docs.text:
1. If you get no records, broaden the filters.
  2. If results are empty, try a different factor or longer time window.
  3. If data fails to load, check the Supabase-related guides.
  4. If the UI changed, check the Streamlit guide for maintainers.

docs.title: 13. Write up your experiment the same way every time
docs.text:
1. State your research question.
  2. Note the run label and list the factors and directions.
  3. List your sidebar settings.
  4. Report the main numbers.
  5. Explain the result.
  6. Note any follow-up test you would run.

docs.title: 14. Reference
docs.text:
Use this section if you want a quick understanding of what the app is doing behind the scenes.

  1. Factor categories include momentum, value, profitability, quality, and growth.
  2. The Results tab is where you verify the backtest output.
  3. The app compares your strategy with benchmark behavior.
  4. Returns come from the dataset's next-year return field.
  5. Delisting behavior changes the outcome, so keep that setting recorded in every experiment.
  6. The Factor Lake Supabase Project is the backing data source.

docs.title: 15. Use WRDS mode
docs.text:
WRDS mode is a second data source next to Legacy. It backtests on point-in-time data built from WRDS (CRSP, Compustat, IBES and the Russell 2000 holdings of the IWM fund), and rebalances semi-annually (June, December), quarterly (March, June, September, December) or monthly, at month ends. Legacy is unchanged: annual rebalancing on the 9/30 data, with the same results as before.

Point in time. At each rebalance date the universe is the Russell 2000 members known on that date, the factors use only data public by then, and returns start after the date. Each holding period is buy and hold until the next rebalance.

docs.title: Run a WRDS backtest
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, set Data Source to WRDS. It is only available when the app is connected to AWS Lambda, because WRDS backtests run there; otherwise it is greyed out with a note.
  2. Switching the data source clears the selected factors, because the two modes offer different factors.
  3. Pick the rebalancing frequency (Quarterly by default) and the start and end years (2008 to 2026). The backtest covers those calendar years, and the caption under the years shows the rebalances, for example "12 quarterly rebalances, 2009-12 to 2012-09; holds to 2012-12".
  4. Weighting, factor combination, sector filter, fossil fuel filter and initial AUM work as in Legacy. The portfolio buys the top 10%, as in Legacy. There is no delisting option (see below).
  5. Add factors on the Analysis tab. They are grouped as Momentum, Value, Profitability, Quality, Growth, Risk, Analyst and Size, and each has a default direction and a tooltip. Factors that default to "Lower is better" say why.
  6. Click Run Portfolio Analysis. There is no Load Market Data step: the backtest reads the WRDS data in AWS.

docs.title: Read WRDS results
docs.text:
The results have Legacy's sections, tiles, tables and charts, on dates instead of years:

  • The run's tab reads e.g. "Run 2: WRDS, Quarterly".
  • Holdings and Ranks: pick a rebalance date to see what was held from that date, with weights, returns and factor values in percent as in Legacy, and a CSV download. All ranked stocks on this date ranks every stock the strategy could buy on that date.
  • Legacy's growth chart against IWM (Russell 2000), IWN (Value) and IWO (Growth), and below it each period's return.
  • Period-by-Period Performance: Legacy's Year-by-Year table with one row per period (switch to By calendar year for yearly returns). Then the cohort comparison, the statistics annualized by the frequency (the caption says how), and a win/loss table per period, e.g. Quarterly Win/Loss Summary.
  • The Analysis ID shares a WRDS run exactly like a Legacy one.

docs.title: How WRDS mode treats delistings and gaps
docs.text:
• Delistings: CRSP delisting returns are included. After a stock delists, its money earns the risk-free rate until the next rebalance.
  • Missing returns: a month without a return (not a delisting) counts as 0%. The results say how many stock-months that was.
  • Risk-free rate: Fama-French one-month T-bill. A month it is not published yet is filled from the 3-month T-bill / 12, and the results list those months.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Sectors use today's GICS codes, not the codes a company had at the time, so the sector filter is the one input that is not strictly point in time.
  • The benchmarks are ETF total returns (IWM, IWN, IWO): they include dividends and are net of the funds' fees. They differ slightly from the index returns Legacy uses, so do not compare Legacy and WRDS numbers directly.
  • The data runs from April 2008 to September 2026. A backtest ending in 2026 holds until September 2026 (semi-annual: June 2026), and one starting in 2008 starts with the first rebalance month in the data.
  • The Data Viewer shows Legacy data only.

docs.title: Streamlit Admin Workflow
docs.text: Use this guide when you need to keep the production Factor-Lake Streamlit App running correctly.

docs.title: 1. Know the production path
docs.text:
1. Source of truth lives in the Factor-Lake GitHub Repo.
  2. Production app runs from app/streamlit_app.py.
  3. Data comes from the Factor Lake Supabase Project.
  4. Deploys happen through Streamlit Cloud.

docs.title: 2. Check the app after every merge
docs.text:
1. Confirm the change is merged to main.
  2. Open the Streamlit Cloud app dashboard.
  3. Confirm the latest commit is the one you expect.
  4. Wait for the build or restart to finish.
  5. Open the live app URL.

docs.title: 3. Run the production smoke test
docs.text:
1. Leave the default sidebar settings in place.
  2. Select at least one factor in Analysis.
  3. Click Load Market Data.
  4. Click Run Portfolio Analysis.
  5. Confirm the Results tab renders metrics and charts.
  6. Change one factor or direction and run again. Confirm a second run tab appears and is selected, and that clicking the first tab still shows its original settings.

docs.title: 4. If the app did not redeploy
docs.text:
1. Sign in to Streamlit Cloud with your GitHub account, then open the app logs from the app control panel.
  2. Check for import, dependency, or secret errors.
  3. Confirm pyproject.toml includes new dependencies.
  4. Trigger a restart or redeploy from the control panel if needed.
  5. Re-test the app after the fix.

docs.title: 5. Manage secrets safely
docs.text:
1. Keep SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_KEY in Streamlit Cloud secrets for production.
  2. Keep .env local for development.
  3. Never commit real secrets.
  4. After any secret change, rerun the smoke test.

docs.title: 6. Review app settings when needed
docs.text:
1. Open the Streamlit Cloud app settings.
  2. Review app visibility and access.
  3. Review restart and resource settings.
  4. Review any deployment-related configuration.
  5. Use caching or usage windows if you need to reduce pressure on the app.

docs.title: Data load error
docs.text:
1. Check the app logs.
  2. Check the Supabase project status.
  3. Confirm the secrets are correct.
  4. Confirm the table and required columns still exist.

docs.title: App loads but analysis fails
docs.text:
1. Check for missing dependencies or import errors.
  2. Check whether the schema changed.
  3. Confirm the factor mappings still match the data.
  4. Re-test after the fix.

docs.title: 8. Check docs deploys when docs change
docs.text:
1. Open GitHub Actions in the Factor-Lake GitHub Repo.
  2. Confirm Deploy MkDocs to GitHub Pages passed.
  3. Open the published docs site.
  4. Confirm the new guide appears under Guides.

docs.title: 9. Finish a semester handoff
docs.text:
1. Confirm app access still works.
  2. Confirm Supabase credentials are still active.
  3. Run and record a smoke test.
  4. Share the current access and support path with the course staff.

docs.title: Supabase Maintenance Workflow
docs.text: Use this guide when you need to add, clean, change, verify, or troubleshoot data in the Factor Lake Supabase Project.

docs.title: 1. Know the moving parts
docs.text:
1. The Factor Lake Supabase Project stores the data.
  2. The Factor-Lake Streamlit App reads that data.
  3. src/supabase_client.py controls the data fetch path.
  4. app/streamlit_utils.py calls the fetch path during app startup.
  5. app/streamlit_config.py and src/factor_registry.py define column mappings used by the app.

docs.title: 2. Use the right access model
docs.text:
1. Use SUPABASE_URL and SUPABASE_KEY for the app.
  2. Use the anon/public key for read-only app usage.
  3. Keep service role keys out of the app and out of git.
  4. Store production secrets in Streamlit Cloud and local secrets in .env.

docs.title: 3. Add or bulk-upload data
docs.text:
Use the dedicated upload workflow in Supabase Upload Tool.

Use this maintenance guide for operational checks after upload (schema compatibility, policies, logs, and app validation).

docs.title: 4. Change which table the app uses
docs.text:
1. Open src/supabase_client.py.
  2. Find SupabaseManager.fetch_all_data(table_name='Full Precision Test').
  3. Change the default table name if you want the app to read a different table.
  4. Confirm that the new table still has the fields the app expects.
  5. Run the app and load data.
  6. Run the integration tests.

docs.title: 5. Keep schema compatibility intact
docs.text:
1. Preserve Ticker or Ticker-Region format/type.
  2. Preserve Year format/type.
  3. Preserve Ending_Price and Next-Years_Return format/type.
  4. Keep factor columns in sync with app/streamlit_config.py and src/factor_registry.py.
  5. If you rename a column, update code and retest immediately.

docs.title: 6. Maintain the delisting mapping table
docs.text:
1. Keep last_price_mapping aligned with the code.
  2. Preserve the source fields ticker, last_date, and last_price unless you are also updating src/supabase_client.py.
  3. Confirm the app still merges Delist_Date and Delist_Price correctly.

docs.title: 7. Review policies and logs
docs.text:
1. Check RLS policies when access changes.
  2. Keep read policies broad enough for the app to work.
  3. Avoid broad write access.
  4. Use Supabase logs when app data loads fail.

docs.title: 8. Troubleshoot a broken data load
docs.text:
1. Check the Factor-Lake Streamlit App logs.
  2. Check Supabase logs for rejected queries.
  3. Confirm the secrets are correct.
  4. Confirm the table exists.
  5. Confirm the required columns still exist.
  6. Run the failing query manually in SQL Editor.

docs.title: 9. Make a safe schema change
docs.text:
1. Make the change in development or staging first.
  2. Verify row counts and field types.
  3. Update app mappings if needed.
  4. Run integration tests.
  5. Run the Streamlit smoke test.
  6. Deploy only after the app still works.

docs.title: 10. Delete a table safely
docs.text:
1. Confirm no app code uses the table.
  2. Confirm no tests depend on the table.
  3. Export a backup.
  4. Delete the table in non-production first.
  5. Verify the app and tests still pass.
  6. Delete in production only after that check.

docs.title: 11. Verify a Supabase change
docs.text:
1. Run tests/integration/test_supabase.py.
  2. Open the Streamlit app.
  3. Click Load Market Data.
  4. Run Portfolio Analysis.
  5. Confirm the Results tab renders.
  6. Check row counts and numeric ranges.

docs.title: 12. What success looks like
docs.text: You are done when the app loads data cleanly, the tests pass, the schema matches the code, and the production app still runs after the change.

docs.title: 13. Related guides
docs.text:
1. Supabase Setup
  2. Supabase Upload Tool
  3. Streamlit Admin Guide
  4. Deployment

docs.title: 14. Reference
docs.text:
Use this section when you need the background details that support the workflow above.

  1. The app reads from src/supabase_client.py.
  2. The app startup path passes through app/streamlit_utils.py.
  3. Factor labels and column names are mapped in app/streamlit_config.py and src/factor_registry.py.
  4. The default table is Full Precision Test unless code changes it.
  5. last_price_mapping supplies delisting fields that the client merges into the dataset.
  6. Common required fields include Ticker, Year, Ending_Price, and Next-Years_Return.
  7. Integration tests in tests/integration/test_supabase.py should be kept aligned with any schema change.

docs.title: Supabase Credentials Setup Workflow
docs.text: Use this guide to get the Streamlit app connected to the Supabase project on your local machine.

docs.title: 1. Open the project links
docs.text:
• Factor Lake Supabase Project
  • Factor-Lake GitHub Repo
  • Factor-Lake Streamlit App

docs.title: 2. Confirm the credentials you will use
docs.text:
Your project should use the current Supabase values provided in the Supabase project:

  • URL: https://-----.supabase.co
  • Key: sb_publishable_-----

You can find them here:

  • Click on the word copy underneath the project name in the main page and copy the URL.
  • For the key, locate Project settings in the side bar -> then click API Keys.

docs.title: Supabase key types (quick reference)
docs.text:
• Publishable key: Intended for client-side or public app contexts with RLS enforcement.
  • Secret keys: Server-side keys for trusted backend environments only.
  • Legacy anon key: Older public key format used in existing setups; similar purpose to publishable key.
  • Service role key: Admin-level server key that bypasses RLS; use only for controlled backend/admin operations.

docs.title: 3. Create your local .env file
docs.text:
1. Open the repo root.
  2. Create a file named .env if it does not already exist.

  3. Add these values to the file:

    env SUPABASE_URL=your-url-here SUPABASE_KEY=your-key-here

  4. Save the file.

  5. Confirm .env stays local and is not committed to git.

docs.title: 4. Start the app locally
docs.text:
1. Open a terminal in the repo root.

  2. Run the Streamlit app:

    bash streamlit run app/streamlit_app.py

  3. Wait for the browser to open.

  4. Confirm the app starts without credential errors.

docs.title: 5. Load data in the app
docs.text:
1. In the sidebar, select Supabase (Cloud) as the data source.
  2. Click Load Data.
  3. Wait for the success message.
  4. Confirm the dataset loads into the app without errors.

docs.title: 6. Verify the setup worked
docs.text:
1. Restart the app once after editing .env if needed.
  2. Re-open the app.
  3. Click Load Data again.
  4. Confirm the message says data loaded successfully.

docs.title: 7. Update credentials when they change
docs.text:
1. Edit .env.
  2. Replace SUPABASE_URL and/or SUPABASE_KEY with the new values.
  3. Save the file.
  4. Restart streamlit run app/streamlit_app.py.
  5. Load data again to confirm the new credentials work.

docs.title: 8. Use Colab only if you still need it
docs.text:
1. Open colab_setup.ipynb.
  2. Confirm the notebook is still appropriate for your use case.
  3. Run the notebook cells only if you are using the Colab path.

docs.title: 9. Keep credentials safe
docs.text:
1. Never commit real secrets.
  2. Keep .env local.
  3. Remove credentials from any shareable notebook or demo artifact.
  4. Use the publishable key only in the allowed client-side context.

docs.title: 10. Troubleshoot the common failures
docs.text:
1. If you see a connection failure, check your internet access and the Supabase project status.
  2. If you see an authentication failure, confirm the key is correct and not expired.
  3. If the app cannot find .env, make sure it is in the repo root next to app/.

docs.title: 11. What success looks like
docs.text: You are done when the app starts, Supabase (Cloud) loads data successfully, and the analysis workflow can continue without credential-related errors.

docs.title: 12. Reference
docs.text:
Use this section when you need to remember how the setup is wired.

  1. Local development reads credentials from .env in the repo root.
  2. app/streamlit_app.py loads the credentials automatically when the app starts.
  3. The publishable key is the expected client-side key for the app workflow.
  4. colab_setup.ipynb is only relevant if you are still using the Colab path.
  5. The Streamlit app should only need the credentials you placed in .env or Streamlit Cloud secrets.
