docs.title: Supabase Upload Tool Workflow
docs.text: Use this guide when you need to create Supabase table(s) and upload local files with the wrapper script at tools/run_data_upload_supabase.sh.

docs.title: 1. Know what this tool does
docs.text:
1. Accepts a single file path or a folder path.
  2. Supports .csv, .xlsx, .xls, and .parquet.
  3. Creates one table per file.
  4. Defaults table names to file names without extensions.
  5. Enables RLS and adds a public read policy (anon and authenticated) for each created table.
  6. Uploads data in chunks and validates row counts after upload.

docs.title: 2. Confirm prerequisites
docs.text:
1. You have SUPABASE_URL and a service role key.
  2. You can run from repo root (D:/Factor-Lake on Windows or /mnt/d/Factor-Lake in WSL).
  3. Sync the project environment first: uv sync --group dev
  4. Upload format dependencies are included in pyproject.toml and installed by uv sync: pandas, supabase, openpyxl (.xlsx), xlrd (.xls), and pyarrow (.parquet).

docs.title: 3. Run the one-time Supabase SQL setup
docs.text:
This tool executes DDL via RPC. In Supabase SQL Editor, run:

create or replace function public.execute_sql(sql text)
returns void
language plpgsql
security definer
set search_path = public
as $$
begin
  execute sql;
end;
$$;

grant execute on function public.execute_sql(text) to service_role;

docs.title: 4. Choose input and table naming behavior
docs.text:
1. Single file input: If TABLE_NAME is omitted, the table name is the file name without extension.
  2. Folder input: The tool scans supported files and creates one table per file name.
  3. Optional TABLE_NAME: Works as an override for single-file uploads only.

docs.title: 5. Run the upload command
docs.text:
General command form:

bash tools/run_data_upload_supabase.sh \
  [--supabase-url <SUPABASE_URL>] \
  [--supabase-service-role-key <SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY>] \
  <FILE_PATH_OR_FOLDER> \
  [TABLE_NAME] \
  [EXTRA_ARGS...]

WSL + Windows Python example:

cd /mnt/d/Factor-Lake && \
PYTHON_BIN="/mnt/c/Users/<you>/anaconda3/envs/<env>/python.exe" \
bash tools/run_data_upload_supabase.sh \
  --supabase-url "https://<project-ref>.supabase.co" \
  --supabase-service-role-key "<service-role-key>" \
  "C:/Users/<you>/Downloads/data.xlsx"

Folder upload example (common for parquet):

cd /mnt/d/Factor-Lake && \
PYTHON_BIN="/mnt/c/Users/<you>/anaconda3/envs/<env>/python.exe" \
bash tools/run_data_upload_supabase.sh \
  --supabase-url "https://<project-ref>.supabase.co" \
  --supabase-service-role-key "<service-role-key>" \
  "C:/Users/<you>/Downloads/parquets"

Environment-variable mode:

export SUPABASE_URL="https://<project-ref>.supabase.co"
export SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY="<service-role-key>"
bash tools/run_data_upload_supabase.sh "C:/Users/<you>/Downloads/data.parquet"

docs.title: 6. Understand the execution flow
docs.text:
1. Resolve input path(s).
  2. Derive table name(s).
  3. Build and run create-table SQL.
  4. Enable RLS and apply public read policy.
  5. Reload PostgREST schema cache when needed.
  6. Upload batches with retry for schema-cache lag.
  7. Validate upload count and preview rows.

docs.title: 7. Troubleshoot common failures
docs.text:
1. No such file or directory for script: Run from repo root and call tools/run_data_upload_supabase.sh.
  2. python: command not found: Set PYTHON_BIN explicitly.
  3. PGRST202 function not found: Run the SQL setup in Section 3.
  4. PGRST205 table not found in schema cache: Retry; schema reload and retry logic are built in.
  5. Excel dependency error for openpyxl/xlrd or parquet engine error for pyarrow: Re-sync dependencies in the same environment: uv sync --group dev.

docs.title: 8. Verify the upload result
docs.text:
1. Confirm upload batch logs show success.
  2. Confirm row count output is greater than zero.
  3. In Supabase Table Editor, verify the table exists and has rows.
  4. Confirm read access works for anon and authenticated roles.

docs.title: 9. What success looks like
docs.text: You are done when the table(s) are created, data is uploaded, row counts look correct, and read access works with RLS enabled.

docs.title: 10. Related guides
docs.text:
1. Supabase Setup
  2. Supabase Maintenance
  3. Deployment

docs.title: 11. Reference
docs.text:
1. Wrapper script: tools/run_data_upload_supabase.sh
  2. Upload engine: tools/data_upload_supabase.py
  3. Supported input extensions: .csv, .xlsx, .xls, .parquet
  4. Table naming default: file name without extension

docs.title: WRDS mode: design
docs.text:
Status: built (all six stages, branch feature/wrds-mode), validated on the dev function sysen5900-factor-lake-backtest-dev. The review's final decisions are in Decisions and are worked into the sections below; where the build differs from the first design, the section says so ("As built" notes in 6, 7 and 8, and the stage table in 10). Using WRDS mode: DOCS/FACTOR_LAKE_USER_GUIDE.md, section 15. Running and deploying it: DOCS/AWS_LAMBDA_BACKTESTS.md, section 9, with the validation table.

WRDS mode is a second data source next to today's data (called Legacy below). It backtests on the point-in-time WRDS panel (pipeline/DATA_DICTIONARY.md) with semi-annual, quarterly or monthly rebalancing, and it runs only in AWS Lambda: the app sends the job and shows the result. Legacy keeps working exactly as it does today.

Contents:

  1. Where Legacy and WRDS split
  2. WRDS factors and sectors
  3. Rebalance dates and look-ahead rules
  4. Benchmarks and metrics
  5. Jobs, cache keys, saved IDs and holdings files
  6. How Lambda loads the WRDS data, with measurements
  7. The vectorized engine and the Legacy match test
  8. Each feature in WRDS mode, and the app without Lambda
  9. Test plan, open questions and risks
  10. Stages and files

A rule for this document and the code that follows: the WRDS data is licensed, so no statistics of the data (row counts, coverage, returns) go into the repo (see pipeline/README.md). The measurements in section 6 are file sizes, memory and run times only.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Decided in the stage 1 review:

# Question Decision Where 1 Delisting during a quarter or half year The money is held as cash earning the risk-free rate until the next rebalance 3.3 2 Ranked stocks A new ranked job that ranks every stock on one rebalance date at a time 5.1, 8 3 Fossil fuel filter Keep the Legacy mapping (the GICS and SIC codes in 2.3; Oil & Gas Storage & Transportation is not excluded) 2.3 4 Default directions where research is mixed Lower is better for all of them. The 1-month factor is named "1-Month Return (Reversal)". Every tooltip that defaults to Lower says why in one short sentence 2.1 5 Unclassified stocks Left out when the sector filter is on 2.2 6 Today's GICS codes for the sector filter Accepted, documented as a limitation 2.2, R3 7 Defaults Quarterly, 2008-2026 8 8 Missing return without a delisting 0% for that month; the result reports how many stock-months that was 3.3 9 ETF total-return benchmarks Accepted, labelled for example "IWM (ETF, total return)" 4.1 10 Missing risk-free month Filled with tbill_3m / 12, and the filled months are flagged in the result 4.1 11 Top % Fixed at 10%, as in Legacy 5.1 - Legacy invariant (correction) Legacy results must not change; its code version and cache keys may. Routing WRDS jobs may edit a file in ENGINE_SOURCES (for example backtest_jobs.py) 1.2

docs.title: 1.1 The split points
docs.text: Layer Legacy (unchanged) WRDS (new) Where the choice is made Sidebar today's controls Data source, frequency, GICS sectors, no delisting option, no Lambda switch settings['data_mode'], new key; Legacy controls are drawn by the same code with the same widget keys Factor list FACTOR_METADATA WRDS_FACTOR_METADATA (section 2) render_factor_selection(data_mode) Run run_backtest_logic (local or Lambda) run_wrds_backtest (Lambda only) one if at the top of run_backtest_logic; the Legacy body below it is not edited Job build_job (src/backtest_jobs.py) build_wrds_job (src/wrds_jobs.py) the job's data_mode key: absent means Legacy Lambda BacktestService.run WrdsBacktestService.run one dispatch on job.get('data_mode') in BacktestService.handle_event Engine src/backtest_engine.py src/wrds_engine.py (vectorized) separate modules Data full_precision_test.parquet, last_price_mapping.parquet wrds_2026_10/factor_panel_monthly.parquet, returns_monthly.parquet, market_monthly.parquet the service that runs the job Benchmarks, metrics src/benchmarks.py, src/performance_metrics.py src/wrds_metrics.py (IWM, IWN, IWO, Fama-French rf) separate modules Results tab render_results_tab render_wrds_results_tab (new app/components/wrds_results.py, reusing Legacy's render helpers read-only) run['data_mode'] Saved IDs backtest-results/<hash>.json the same file layout, plus <hash>.holdings.parquet the saved job's data_mode Data Viewer Legacy data stays Legacy not split

docs.title: 1.2 How Legacy results stay unchanged
docs.text:
The invariant is that Legacy results do not change. Legacy's code version and cache keys may change: editing a file in ENGINE_SOURCES (for example backtest_jobs.py, to route WRDS jobs) changes the code version, so Legacy results are computed once more under new keys, with the same numbers. Old Legacy analysis IDs still open, because opening reads the saved file by its ID and never recomputes it (5.4).

  1. Engine. The Legacy engine (backtest_engine.py, benchmarks.py, performance_metrics.py, universe_selection.py, ...) is not edited. WRDS code lives in new src/wrds_*.py modules that may import Legacy files but do not change them. Files that only route jobs, such as backtest_jobs.py, may get a WRDS branch.
  2. Job. Legacy jobs are still built by build_job, which reads only the keys it knows. The sidebar's Legacy settings are exactly as on main (no data_mode key), and a Legacy job never has a data_mode key.
  3. Data. Legacy reads the same two files. The WRDS data sits in its own folder (factor-lake-data/wrds_2026_10/), so publishing it changes nothing Legacy reads.
  4. Local Legacy runs. run_backtest_logic's Legacy body, load_and_process_data and select_universe are not edited. The WRDS branch is decided before the Legacy code runs.
  5. Pinned results. tests/unit/test_legacy_pinned.py runs fixed Legacy jobs (Mixing and Integrating, all three delisting strategies, equal and cap weight, a sector filter, a cohort comparison) through build_job and run_job. It compares the whole result, holdings included, with tests/fixtures/legacy_pinned_results.json, which was captured from main (c063100) before any WRDS code existed.
  6. Tests. Every existing test passes without being edited. New behaviour gets new test files. If an existing app test has to change because the sidebar gained a widget, that is a sign the Legacy path changed, and the change is reviewed as such.

docs.title: 2.1 Factor list
docs.text:
Every factor is a column of factor_panel_monthly.parquet whose value at month end t was public by t (data dictionary, "Point in time"). The display names describe the WRDS definition, so they are not Legacy's names (no "9/30 Data"). Direction is the default when the factor is added: Higher = buy the highest values ('top'), Lower = buy the lowest ('bottom').

Group Column Display name Default Tooltip Momentum mom_12_1 12-1 Mo Momentum Higher Return over the past 12 months, skipping the most recent month. Momentum mom_12m 12-Mo Momentum Higher Return over the past 252 trading days. Momentum mom_6m 6-Mo Momentum Higher Return over the past 126 trading days. Momentum mom_1m 1-Month Return (Reversal) Lower Return over the past 21 trading days. Lower is better: last month's losers tend to rebound the next month. Value f_book_to_price Book/Price Higher Book equity divided by the company's market cap today. Value f_earnings_to_price Earnings/Price Higher Trailing 12-month earnings divided by market cap. Value f_sales_to_price Sales/Price Higher Trailing 12-month revenue divided by market cap. Value f_fcf_yield FCF Yield Higher Trailing 12-month free cash flow divided by market cap. Value f_dividend_yield Dividend Yield Higher Trailing 12-month dividends divided by market cap. Value f_ebitda_to_ev EBITDA/EV Higher Trailing 12-month EBITDA divided by enterprise value. Value f_ebit_to_ev EBIT/EV Higher Trailing 12-month EBIT divided by enterprise value. Value f_sales_to_ev Sales/EV Higher Trailing 12-month revenue divided by enterprise value. Value f_forward_ep Forward E/P (FY1) Higher Analyst consensus EPS for this fiscal year divided by price. Value f_forward_ep_fy2 Forward E/P (FY2) Higher Analyst consensus EPS for next fiscal year divided by price. Value f_forward_cfp Forward Cash Flow/P Higher Analyst consensus cash flow per share divided by price. Value f_forward_sales_to_ev Forward Sales/EV Higher Analyst consensus sales divided by enterprise value. Value f_forward_ebitda_to_ev Forward EBITDA/EV Higher Analyst consensus EBITDA divided by enterprise value. Profitability f_roe ROE Higher Trailing 12-month net income divided by book equity. Profitability f_roa ROA Higher Trailing 12-month net income divided by total assets. Profitability f_gross_profitability Gross Profitability Higher Revenue minus cost of goods sold (trailing 12 months), divided by total assets. Quality f_accruals_to_assets Accruals/Assets Lower Net income minus operating cash flow, over total assets. Lower is better: earnings backed by cash tend to last. Quality f_leverage Debt/Assets Lower Total debt divided by total assets. Lower is better: less debt means less risk of financial distress. Quality f_current_ratio Current Ratio Higher Current assets divided by current liabilities. Quality f_net_share_issuance Net Share Issuance Lower Change in split-adjusted shares outstanding over the past year. Lower is better: companies that issue shares tend to trail those that buy them back. Growth f_asset_growth_1yr 1-Yr Asset Growth Lower Total assets vs four quarters earlier. Lower is better: fast-growing companies tend to underperform. Growth f_sales_growth_1yr 1-Yr Sales Growth Higher Trailing 12-month revenue vs a year earlier. Growth f_capex_growth_1yr 1-Yr CapEx Growth Lower Trailing 12-month capex vs a year earlier. Lower is better: companies that ramp up investment tend to underperform. Growth f_rd_to_sales R&D/Sales Higher Trailing 12-month R&D divided by revenue. Risk vol_close_12m 12-Mo Volatility Lower Annualized volatility of daily returns over the past year. Lower is better: calmer stocks have earned as much with less risk. Risk vol_close_6m 6-Mo Volatility Lower Annualized volatility of daily returns over the past 6 months. Lower is better: calmer stocks have earned as much with less risk. Risk vol_close_3m 3-Mo Volatility Lower Annualized volatility of daily returns over the past 3 months. Lower is better: calmer stocks have earned as much with less risk. Risk vol_gk_1m 1-Mo Volatility (High-Low) Lower Garman-Klass volatility from daily open, high, low and close over the past month, annualized. Lower is better: calmer stocks have earned as much with less risk. Risk beta_252d Beta (1-Yr Daily) Lower Market beta from daily excess returns over the past year. Lower is better: low-beta stocks have earned more than their risk suggests. Risk beta_60m Beta (5-Yr Monthly) Lower Market beta from monthly excess returns over the past 5 years. Lower is better: low-beta stocks have earned more than their risk suggests. Analyst f_sue Earnings Surprise (SUE) Higher Change in quarterly EPS vs a year earlier, scaled by its past volatility. Analyst f_analyst_surprise Analyst EPS Surprise Higher Latest reported EPS minus the consensus before it, over price. Analyst f_eps_revision EPS Revisions Higher Analysts revising this year's EPS up minus those revising down, over the number of analysts. Analyst f_eps_dispersion Analyst Disagreement Lower Spread of analysts' EPS estimates relative to their mean. Lower is better: stocks analysts disagree on tend to underperform. Analyst f_ltg Long-Term Growth Forecast Lower Analysts' long-term EPS growth forecast. Lower is better: the most optimistic forecasts tend to disappoint. Size mkt_cap_musd Market Cap Lower Market value of the listed shares. Lower is better: smaller companies have historically earned more.

Left out on purpose:

  • ret_next_1m and delisted_next_month describe the month after t. They are the holding return, never a factor (section 3.3).
  • The _qe columns (f_book_to_price_qe, ...) use Compustat's quarter-end price, which is up to a quarter old at t. The table above uses today's price instead.
  • vol_close_1m, vol_gk_3m, vol_gk_6m, vol_gk_12m repeat factors already listed.
  • rv_multiples_monthly.parquet (within-industry percentiles) is a separate file. It can be added later without changing the design.

Where the list lives:

  • app/streamlit_config.py gets WRDS_FACTOR_METADATA and WRDS_FACTOR_GROUPS, in the same shape as FACTOR_METADATA (key, group, column, tooltip, higher_is_better), keyed by display name. Widget keys get a w_ prefix so they never clash with Legacy keys.
  • src/wrds_factors.py holds WRDS_FACTOR_COLUMNS, the allowlist the Lambda checks jobs against. A test checks that both lists name the same columns.

The factor picker today lays out one column per group, so eight groups need two rows (stage 2).

docs.title: 2.2 Sectors
docs.text:
The sector filter offers the 11 GICS sectors, using the panel's sector_name column (GICS, with the SIC fallback from the data dictionary): Communication Services, Consumer Discretionary, Consumer Staples, Energy, Financials, Health Care, Industrials, Information Technology, Materials, Real Estate, Utilities.

sector_name also has the value Unclassified, for stocks with neither GICS nor a mapped SIC code. These stocks are in the universe when the sector filter is off. They are not offered in the list, so turning the filter on leaves them out (decision 5).

Limitation (decision 6): the panel's GICS code is today's classification, not the historical one (data dictionary), so the sector filter is the one input that is not strictly point in time. A stock that moved sectors is filtered by its current sector for its whole history. The sector list's tooltip says so (risk R3).

docs.title: 2.3 Fossil fuel filter
docs.text: Legacy excludes five FactSet industries. WRDS mode excludes the matching GICS sub-industries (gsubind): 10101010 Oil & Gas Drilling, 10101020 Oil & Gas Equipment & Services, 10102010 Integrated Oil & Gas, 10102020 Oil & Gas Exploration & Production, 10102030 Oil & Gas Refining & Marketing, 10102050 Coal & Consumable Fuels. Where GICS is missing, it excludes SIC 1221, 1222, 1231 (coal), 1311 (crude oil and gas), 1381, 1382, 1389 (oil and gas field services) and 2911 (refining). This keeps Legacy's mapping (decision 3): 10102040 Oil & Gas Storage & Transportation is not in Legacy's list, so it is kept.

docs.title: 3.1 Rebalance months
docs.text:
Frequency Rebalance months Periods per year (k) Semi-annual Jun, Dec 2 Quarterly Mar, Jun, Sep, Dec 4 Monthly every month 12

A rebalance date is the panel's date in that month: the last CRSP trading day of the month, not the calendar month end. The UI shows the real dates.

docs.title: 3.2 Start and end years
docs.text:
The sidebar still asks for a start year and an end year, from 2008 to 2026. The backtest covers the calendar years from start to end, within the data's bounds (first panel month 2008-04, last month with returns 2026-09):

  • The first rebalance is the December month end of start_year - 1. When that is before the data starts, it is the first rebalance month in the data instead.
  • The last holding period ends at the December month end of end_year. When that is after the data ends, it ends at the last rebalance month whose whole holding period is in the data. There are no partial periods.
  • Rebalances are every rebalance month between the two. Each holding period runs from one rebalance date to the next.
  • start_year == end_year is allowed (one calendar year). start_year > end_year is fixed by the sidebar as today. A range with no complete period is rejected with a message.
Run Rebalance dates Holding periods cover Monthly, 2008-2026 2008-04 ... 2026-08 (221) May 2008 - Sep 2026 Quarterly, 2008-2026 2008-06 ... 2026-06 (73) Jul 2008 - Sep 2026 Semi-annual, 2008-2026 2008-06 ... 2025-12 (36) Jul 2008 - Jun 2026 Quarterly, 2010-2012 2009-12 ... 2012-09 (12) Jan 2010 - Dec 2012 Monthly, 2015-2015 2014-12 ... 2015-11 (12) Jan 2015 - Dec 2015

src/wrds_calendar.py holds this rule as a pure function that works on year-month values, so the sidebar can show "Rebalances: 2009-12 to 2012-09 (12 quarterly)" without any data. The Lambda then maps each month to the panel's trading date and rejects a job whose months are not in the data. The data bounds (2008-04, 2026-09) are constants in src/wrds_calendar.py, and a data test checks them against the files.

docs.title: 3.3 Look-ahead rules
docs.text:
At each rebalance date t:

  1. Universe. The stocks are the panel rows at date t: the Russell 2000 members of the latest IWM snapshot that was public by t (snapshot_eff_dt <= t). The engine never filters on anything dated after t. In particular, a stock is not dropped because it later has no return or delists.
  2. Buyable. A stock needs prc > 0 and mkt_cap_musd > 0 at t. Both are known at t.
  3. Factors. Only allowlisted columns (section 2.1), and only their values at t. The pipeline guarantees these were public by t (Compustat report date, IBES statistics date, announcement date). Z-scores use only the stocks at t.
  4. Weights. Market-cap weights use mkt_cap_musd at t.
  5. Returns start after t. A position bought at the close on t earns the stock's monthly returns for the months after t, up to and including the next rebalance date t'. These are ret_m from returns_monthly.parquet for each month in (t, t'], for every frequency. The panel's ret_next_1m holds the same values for one month, but the loader never reads it, so no column about the month after t is ever in memory next to the factors. returns_monthly keeps a stock's rows after it leaves the index, so a stock that drops out mid-period is still held to t'.
  6. Delisting. CRSP's delisting return is included in the delisting month's ret_m. A stock has no rows after it delists. For the rest of the period, its money is held as cash earning the risk-free rate until the next rebalance (decision 1), and the position is marked Delisted.
  7. Missing return. If a held stock has no return for a month and has not delisted (it stopped trading, or CRSP has no price), that month counts as 0% and the position is still held. The result reports how many stock-months that was (missing_return_stock_months; decision 8).
  8. Benchmarks compound over the same months (t, t'] (section 4).

Section 9.1 lists the tests for these rules.

docs.title: 4.1 Benchmarks
docs.text:
All benchmarks come from market_monthly.parquet, compounded over each holding period's months (t, t']:

Role Column Shown as Benchmark iwm_total_ret IWM (ETF, total return) Value iwn_total_ret IWN (ETF, total return) Growth iwo_total_ret IWO (ETF, total return) Risk-free rf Fama-French one-month T-bill
  • These are ETF total returns (dividends in, fund fees out). Legacy uses index returns, so the two modes' benchmarks are not the same numbers.
  • The Fama-French rf is published a few weeks late, so the newest month can be missing. A missing month is filled with that month end's 3-month T-bill yield divided by 12, tbill_3m / 12, and the result flags the filled months (rf_filled_months; decision 10).
  • benchmark_index is not part of a WRDS job: the benchmark is always IWM.

docs.title: 4.2 Metrics
docs.text:
src/wrds_metrics.py returns the same metric keys as compute_comprehensive_metrics, so the Results tab's grids work unchanged. It works on period returns, with k periods per year (section 3.1):

Metric WRDS definition Legacy (k = 1) Period returns portfolio, benchmarks and rf per holding period yearly CAGR (final / initial) ** (k / n) - 1 for n periods n years Volatility (raw, excess) std(ddof=1) * sqrt(k) the same with k = 1 Sharpe mean(excess) / std(excess) * sqrt(k) the same with k = 1 Information ratio mean(active) / std(active) * sqrt(k) the same with k = 1 Beta slope of period excess returns (not annualized) the same Max drawdown on the portfolio value after each period the same Win rate share of periods beating the benchmark ("period win rate") yearly Calendar-year returns each calendar year's periods compounded (new) none

With k = 1 the formulas are Legacy's. A test feeds the same returns to both functions and checks that every shared key matches (section 9.1). The result also says frequency, periods_per_year and risk_free_rate_source: "Fama-French one-month T-bill".

docs.title: 5. Jobs, cache keys, saved IDs and holdings files
5.1 WRDS jobs
docs.text:
A WRDS job is plain JSON like a Legacy job, built by build_wrds_job and checked by validate_wrds_job (src/wrds_jobs.py):

Field Values Notes kind backtest, cohort, ranked ranked is new (section 8) data_mode wrds absent in Legacy jobs wrds_job_version 1 for future changes to the schema factors allowlisted columns, in the order added factor_directions {column: 'top' or 'bottom'} factor_labels {column: display name} shown when an ID is opened frequency semiannual, quarterly, monthly start_year, end_year 2008-2026 section 3.2 initial_aum > 0 top_pct 10.0 fixed, as in Legacy (decision 11) use_market_cap_weight bool factor_combination mixing, integrating restrict_fossil_fuels bool section 2.3 selected_sectors sorted GICS sector names cohort_pct number for cohort, else null rebalance_date YYYY-MM for ranked, else null must be one of the run's rebalance months

There is no delisting_strategy (returns include delisting returns) and no benchmark_index.

docs.title: 5.2 Cache key
docs.text:
The key is computed by the unchanged job_hash(job, data_version, code_version), so it is the same kind of 64-character SHA-256 as Legacy's:

  • job: the WRDS job. Its data_mode key means it can never equal a Legacy job.
  • data_version: the WRDS folder name plus the S3 ETags of the three files the engine reads, for example wrds_2026_10|factor_panel_monthly.parquet:<etag>|returns_monthly.parquet:<etag>|market_monthly.parquet:<etag>. A new WRDS pull goes into a new folder, so it gives new keys.
  • code_version: a hash of WRDS_ENGINE_SOURCES (the src/wrds_*.py modules plus the shared files they import, such as factor_utils.py), computed the same way as code_version().

docs.title: 5.3 Where results are stored
docs.text:
Object Contents backtest-results/<hash>.json the same envelope as Legacy, {'format': 2, 'job': ..., 'result': ...}. A WRDS backtest result holds everything except the holdings, plus holdings: {'file', 'dates', 'rows', 'bytes'} backtest-results/<hash>.holdings.parquet WRDS backtest holdings, one row group per rebalance date (section 5.5)
  • Both are under backtest-results/, so the existing 90-day lifecycle rule and the Lambda role's write permission already cover them.
  • The Parquet file is written before the JSON, so a cache hit (the JSON exists) normally has its holdings. A cached backtest whose holdings file is missing anyway (deleted by hand, or expired first) is computed again rather than shown without holdings. With the Lambda role's s3:ListBucket missing, S3 answers 403 for a missing file, which counts as missing too.
  • The result JSON's holdings entry is {'file': 'backtest-results/<hash>.holdings.parquet', 'bytes', 'dates', 'rows'}: the row groups' dates (rebalance dates on which something was bought) in order, and their row counts.
  • The WRDS code version hashes WRDS_ENGINE_SOURCES (src/wrds_jobs.py): the wrds_*.py modules plus the shared files they use (backtest_jobs.py, performance_metrics.py, s3_client.py). Legacy's ENGINE_SOURCES list is unchanged, so editing WRDS code never recomputes Legacy results.
  • Without holdings, a monthly result is a few hundred kilobytes, well inside the inline limit, so the S3-link path is rarely needed.

docs.title: 5.4 Saved IDs, old and new
docs.text:
• Old IDs keep opening. Legacy files, their path, decode_saved and SAVED_FORMAT do not change. The app treats a saved job without data_mode as Legacy, exactly as today. Analyses saved before sharing still get today's message.
  • WRDS IDs open through the same "Open a saved analysis" box. load_saved_analysis reads them unchanged (their kind is backtest). open_saved_analysis builds a WRDS run from the job when job.get('data_mode') == 'wrds' (today it reads Legacy-only keys such as delisting_strategy).
  • cohort and ranked IDs are refused with today's message ("This ID belongs to a cohort comparison..."), with the wording widened to cover ranked lists.

docs.title: 5.5 Holdings as Parquet, loaded per date
docs.text:
The holdings file has one row per stock held per rebalance date, sorted by date and rank, with one row group per date.

Columns: rebalance_date, rank, permno, ticker, name, sector, picked_by (Mixing), score, one column per factor (raw value at t), weight, buy_price, dollar_value, period_return, contribution, delisted.

  • A stock picked by several Mixing sleeves is one row, merged the way _build_holdings_rows merges them today.
  • The app renames the columns to Legacy's display headers (Rank, Ticker, Name, Sector, Picked By, Score, factor labels, Weight %, Shares, Buy Price, Dollar Value, Period Return %, Contribution %, Delisted) and adds PERMNO, because two securities can share a ticker on one date.

When the user picks a date, the app reads the file's footer and that date's row group with ranged S3 GETs (src/wrds_holdings.read_holdings_date): one GET of the last 64 KB (the footer, plus a second GET if the footer is bigger), then one GET of exactly that row group's bytes. It caches the table per (file, date) with st.cache_data.

The app reads with its own S3 keys, not a presigned link from Lambda. The app already reads backtest-results/ with its own keys to open saved analyses by ID. A presigned link expires (an hour today), so a shared ID opened later would need a new Lambda call just to get a fresh link. With its own keys, opening an ID and reading any date's holdings never calls Lambda, and nothing expires before the 90-day rule deletes the files. Opening a result therefore downloads only the small JSON, and each date costs one small read. For a 3-factor monthly Mixing run, the prototype's holdings file was 9.0 MB as Parquet (the same rows are about 44 MB as JSON), and reading one date back took about 0.02 s locally.

docs.title: 6. How Lambda loads the WRDS data, with measurements
6.1 Files and columns
docs.text:
File (under factor-lake-data/wrds_2026_10/) Columns read Use factor_panel_monthly.parquet date, permno, ticker, security_name, sector_name, gsubind, siccd, prc, mkt_cap_musd, ret_next_1m, and the 39 allowlisted factor columns (49 of 103) universe, factors, weights, one-month returns returns_monthly.parquet month_end, permno, ret_m, delisted_in_month returns for later months of a period, delisting months market_monthly.parquet month_end, iwm_total_ret, iwn_total_ret, iwo_total_ret, rf, tbill_3m benchmarks, risk-free rate
  • The panel is one zstd row group, so dates cannot be skipped inside the file. The Lambda downloads each file with one GET and decodes only the listed columns. Text columns become pandas categoricals.
  • The Lambda builds a month by permno matrix of ret_m once per container.
  • It keeps the frames for the life of the container, next to the Legacy universe, and reloads them only when the WRDS data version changes, as _load_universe does for Legacy.
  • The folder name is WRDS_DATA_DIR = 'wrds_2026_10' in src/wrds_data.py, overridable with FACTOR_LAKE_WRDS_DIR, which the deploy script sets on the function.
  • prices_daily/ is not needed: every rebalance is at a month end, so monthly returns are enough.

docs.title: 6.2 Measured on the real files
docs.text:
These numbers come from a throwaway prototype of the vectorized engine (section 7), run locally on the files in processed/final/: Windows desktop, Python 3.10, pandas 2.3.3, pyarrow 24.0.0. "Peak" is the process's peak working set.

Step Time Memory Panel file (148.6 MB on disk) read into memory as bytes 0.05 s 220 MB process Decode the 49 needed columns 0.14 s 631 MB peak; the frame itself is 155 MB (for comparison) decode all 103 columns 0.23 s 862 MB process returns_monthly (16.2 MB on disk) and market_monthly, plus the return matrix 0.08 s about 500 MB after the bytes are freed Monthly, Integrating, 2 factors, equal weight (221 periods) 0.73 s Monthly, Mixing, 3 factors, cap weight 1.09 s Monthly, Mixing, 10 factors, equal weight 2.86 s 723 MB peak Quarterly, Integrating, 2 factors / Semi-annual, Mixing, 2 factors 0.25 s / 0.15 s Write a monthly 3-factor Mixing run's holdings as Parquet 0.12 s 9.0 MB file Whole session (load and 7 runs) 8.0 s 728 MB peak

docs.title: 6.3 Estimates for Lambda (monthly run)
docs.text:
Lambda at 3008 MB gets about 2 vCPUs, and pandas mostly uses one core. We assume a core about 1.5 to 2 times slower than the desktop above, and S3 reads in the same region at about 80 to 100 MB/s.

Case Estimate Cold container, first WRDS job: init (as today) + download 165 MB + decode + 3-factor monthly run + holdings write and PUT about 8 to 12 s Warm container, new 3-factor monthly job about 2 to 4 s Warm container, 10-factor monthly Mixing about 5 to 7 s Cohort comparison (two backtests, no holdings) about 2 times a backtest, without the holdings write Ranked list for one date under 1 s warm Cached repeat under 0.5 s, as today Peak memory about 0.8 GB for WRDS, about 1.0 to 1.2 GB with the Legacy universe also warm

docs.title: 6.4 Measured with the stage 3 engine
docs.text:
scripts/check_wrds_engine.py <processed/final folder> runs each case in a fresh process, as a Lambda invocation would, on the same Windows desktop:

Case (monthly, 2008-2026) Load Run Peak memory Holdings table in memory Whole universe, cap weighted (the IWM tracking check) 0.4 s 1.5 s 0.95 GB 41 MB Mixing, 3 factors, equal weight 0.3 s 1.4 s 0.84 GB 21 MB Mixing, 10 factors, equal weight 0.4 s 4.4 s 1.05 GB 57 MB

The tracking check passed (correlation at least 0.99, tracking error at most 3% a year; the values are printed, not stored). Peak memory is above the 0.8 GB estimate of 6.3, because the holdings table and its merges are built in memory, and still about a third of the function's 3008 MB.

On Windows, repeated runs in one process get slower: after one engine run, even a plain numpy argsort benchmark in the same process is about 4 times slower, so the cause is the process's memory allocator, not the engine. Lambda runs Linux, and stage 6 measures warm repeats there.

docs.title: 6.5 Measured in the dev Lambda (stage 4)
docs.text:
The stage 4 code, deployed to the dev function sysen5900-factor-lake-backtest-dev (3008 MB, the course role), driven from the local app. The times are the Lambda REPORT lines, taken from the invocation log tail.

Job Lambda duration Max memory used Result JSON Holdings Parquet Monthly Mixing, 3 factors, 2008-2026, cold container (init 2.6 s, plus the first WRDS data load) 6.8 s 1013 MB 87 KB 23.2 MB The same job again (cache hit) 0.09 s 1013 MB 87 KB Quarterly Mixing, 3 factors, warm 1.1 s 1013 MB 30 KB 7.3 MB Quarterly cohort, 10% (two backtests) 1.4 s 1013 MB 4 KB Ranked list, one date 0.3 s 1013 MB 0.9 MB Legacy backtest, warm 2.3 s 1013 MB

The package is 61.7 MB zipped and 199 MB unzipped (Lambda allows 250 MB). The holdings file is bigger than the 9 MB prototype in 6.2: it has more text columns (name, sector, picked_by), and 221 small row groups compress less well than one large one. That only affects storage: a date is still read with two small ranged GETs. The Legacy result from the dev function matched main's code run locally on the same S3 data, within the 1e-9 relative tolerance of scripts/check_backtest_lambda.py (the largest difference was rounding in the last binary digit, Linux vs Windows).

Recommendation: keep the function at 3008 MB and a 600 s timeout. The memory leaves plenty of headroom, and Lambda's CPU share grows with memory. The measured cold, warm, cached and concurrent runs (stage 6) are in DOCS/AWS_LAMBDA_BACKTESTS.md, section 9: at most about 1.15 GB of memory, a monthly 3-factor run in about 3 s warm, and no slowdown on repeated warm runs on Linux.

docs.title: 7. The vectorized engine and the Legacy match test
7.1 Engine
docs.text:
src/wrds_engine.py works on whole frames, with no per-stock Python loops. It reproduces Legacy's math exactly.

  1. Rebalance rows. The panel rows at the rebalance dates that are buyable and pass the sector and fossil fuel filters.
  2. Scores, for each factor and date, as normalize_series computes them: values to numbers with inf as NaN, winsorized at the 1% and 99% quantiles (groupby('date')[col].transform('quantile', q), the same linear interpolation as Series.quantile), negated for Lower, then z-scored with the date's mean and std(ddof=1), with the same sigma > 1e-12 guard.
  3. Selection. Integrating: the mean of the factors' z-scores for stocks that have every factor. Mixing: each factor's own z-score in its own sleeve. Within each date (and sleeve), stocks are sorted by score, highest first, with ties broken by permno, so every machine picks the same stocks. The top max(1, floor(n * top_pct / 100)) are kept, where n is the number of stocks with a score.
  4. Weights. Equal, or mkt_cap_musd share, within the portfolio (Integrating) or within each sleeve, with each sleeve given 1 / number of factors of the money (Mixing).
  5. Returns. Each position's growth is the product of (1 + monthly return) over the period's months (section 3.3), with delisted money earning rf after the delisting month. The period return is sum(weight * growth) - 1: buy and hold within the period, rebalanced at each rebalance date.
  6. Outputs. Period returns, values, holdings rows (merged per stock as in Legacy), counts of delisted positions and missing-return months, and the metrics (section 4).

As built in stage 3:

  • Result. It has the Legacy result keys (per-period returns in percent under yearly_returns, metrics annualized by frequency). years holds the period boundary dates as YYYY-MM-DD strings, and each yearly_comparisons entry also has period_start, period_end and the year of its end. The extras are rebalance_dates, period_end_dates, cagr, rf_returns, benchmark_labels, rf_filled_months, total_delisted_positions, missing_return_stock_months and empty_rebalance_dates. The Results tab still turns years into ints, so stage 5 renders WRDS runs with dates.
  • Holdings DataFrame. One row per stock per rebalance date. Weights, returns and contributions are decimals (Legacy's rows are percent), and ticker, name and sector are categoricals. Factor values are under their column names; stage 5 maps them to display names.
  • A date with nothing to buy (for example a narrow sector filter): the money earns the risk-free rate for that period, and the date is listed in empty_rebalance_dates.
  • A holding period with a month without benchmark data is refused with an error.
  • Shared code. performance_metrics.compute_comprehensive_metrics gained periods_per_year (default 1: Legacy unchanged, which the pinned Legacy test checks), and S3DataManager gained a public read_bytes. Both files are in ENGINE_SOURCES, so Legacy's code version changes, as the review allowed.

The core (steps 2 to 5) does not depend on the frequency: it takes rows of (date, id, factor values, cap, return for the period), so it can also be run on Legacy's annual data. That is what the match test does.

docs.title: 7.2 Deliberate differences from the Legacy engine
docs.text: Topic Legacy WRDS Stock id ticker (duplicate tickers are deduplicated) permno (two securities can share a ticker) Ties sort order depends on the machine broken by permno Stocks without a price ranked, then skipped when bought (n counts them) not buyable, so not ranked Cap weight with a missing cap weight 0 not buyable Delisting three strategies, Delist_Price and date CRSP delisting return, then cash at rf until the next rebalance

docs.title: 7.3 The match test
docs.text:
tests/unit/test_wrds_engine_matches_legacy.py builds a synthetic Legacy-style frame (Year, Ticker, Ending_Price, Next-Years_Return, Market_Capitalization, several factors with some NaN), with values chosen so that none of the differences in 7.2 apply: every stock has a price, a cap and a return, tickers are unique, and no cut falls inside a block of tied scores. It then:

  • runs rebalance_portfolio (Legacy, zero_return), and
  • runs the WRDS core on the same rows (date = Year, id = ticker code, return = Next-Years_Return / 100, cap = Market_Capitalization),

for Mixing and Integrating, equal and cap weight, mixed directions, and top_pct 2, 10 and 50. It asserts that every year's stocks are the same set, each stock's weight, return and contribution are equal to a relative 1e-12, and the period returns and portfolio values are equal to a relative 1e-12. A second test runs a tied cut and checks that WRDS picks by permno. The metrics test in 4.2 covers the rest of the shared math.

docs.title: 8. Each feature in WRDS mode, and the app without Lambda
docs.text:
Feature WRDS mode Sidebar Data source: Legacy (default) or WRDS. WRDS shows Rebalancing: Semi-annual, Quarterly (default), Monthly; ESG filter; weighting; factor combination; the 11 GICS sectors; the period (2008-2026, with a caption naming the first rebalance and the last period end); initial AUM. The holdings table's order, names and units: Rank (by composite score), Ticker, Name, Sector, Held, Score, per factor its value, z-score and (Mixing) own rank, then Weight %, Price, PERMNO. With "IWM (ETF, total return)", "Value: IWN (ETF, total return)" and "Growth: IWO (ETF, total return)". Below it, the one WRDS addition: each period's return (portfolio bars, the IWM line in Legacy's benchmark style, Visualizations/wrds_plots.py). Its Ranked stocks and Generate Comparison buttons are then disabled with the same note.

docs.title: 9. Test plan, open questions and risks
9.1 Tests (new files; existing tests are not edited)
docs.text:
File Checks test_legacy_pinned.py fixed Legacy jobs give exactly the results they gave on main (section 1.2) test_wrds_calendar.py the rebalance dates in the section 3.2 table for each frequency; data bounds; start == end; out-of-range years rejected; trading-day dates used, not calendar month ends (stage 3, when dates come from the panel) test_wrds_factors.py the app's factor list and the Lambda allowlist match; keys, groups and tooltips; every Lower default says why; the 11 GICS sectors test_wrds_lookahead.py changing any row dated after t leaves the holdings at t unchanged; changing returns changes returns only, never the selection; non-allowlisted columns (ret_next_1m, delisted_next_month, ...) are rejected as factors; a stock that joins later is never held earlier; a stock that leaves mid-period is held to t' with returns_monthly returns; a period's return uses exactly the months in (t, t'] test_wrds_engine.py the Legacy match of section 7.3 (stocks, ranks, scores, weights, returns, Picked By) and per-date z-scores equal to normalize_series; drift within a period, delisting then cash at rf, missing-return months at 0% and counted, rf fill from tbill_3m / 12, benchmarks compounded; sectors, fossil fuel GICS and SIC codes, buyable stocks, permno tie-break, at least one stock; rebalance dates and holding periods per frequency from the 2008 start to the 2026 end; the metrics default equals Legacy and k annualizes volatility, Sharpe and IR test_wrds_service.py the same data from a local folder and a fake S3, only the needed columns decoded; docs.text: # Risk Mitigation R1 An edit to a shared file changes Legacy results test_legacy_pinned.py compares whole Legacy results with main's; WRDS code lives in new modules (a changed Legacy cache key alone is allowed) R2 Look-ahead creeps in through a new factor or filter factor allowlist; look-ahead tests that change future rows R3 The sector filter uses today's GICS documented in the UI tooltip and in this design; historical GICS would need a new pipeline pull R4 Licensed WRDS values are shown in the app (holdings, ranked lists, factor values) and in shared IDs same private bucket and access model as Legacy; no WRDS data in the repo; the Data Viewer stays Legacy; check the WRDS terms before the class demo R5 Big holdings files for many-factor monthly Mixing runs Parquet with one row group per date, read per date, so the app never downloads the whole file R6 Cold starts download about 165 MB one GET per file per container; warm reuse; at most a few seconds in region R7 Rounding differs between the Mac and Lambda ties broken by permno; comparisons use a relative tolerance of 1e-9, as the Legacy check does R8 The 2026-09 data end and the late Fama-French month data bounds in one place with a data test; rf fill flagged in the result R9 Monthly plots and tables with 221 points one date tick per year; no markers over 60 points; scrolling tables; calendar-year view

def plot_portfolio_growth(
    years: List[int],
    port_vals: List[float],
    bench_vals: Optional[List[float]] = None,
    val_vals: Optional[List[float]] = None,
    gro_vals: Optional[List[float]] = None,
    factor_names: Optional[List[str]] = None,
    names: Optional[Dict[str, str]] = None,
    dates: bool = False
) -> go.Figure:
    """
    Constructs a time-series line chart comparing strategy growth against multiple benchmarks.

    This utility provides an interactive visualization of cumulative wealth,
    supporting overlays for market, value, and growth indices.

    Args:
        years: A list of integers representing the timeline years.
        port_vals: Cumulative dollar values for the strategy portfolio.
        bench_vals: Optional cumulative values for the Russell 2000 index.
        val_vals: Optional cumulative values for the Russell 2000 Value Index.
        gro_vals: Optional cumulative values for the Russell 2000 Growth Index.
        factor_names: A list of active factor labels to be included in the chart title.
        names: Benchmark names by role ('benchmark', 'value', 'growth'), Legacy's by default.
        dates: True when `years` are dates (WRDS runs): a date axis with a tick per year.

    Returns:
        go.Figure: The generated Plotly figure object.
    """
    fig = go.Figure()
    names = {**BENCHMARK_NAMES, **(names or {})}
    mode = line_mode(len(years))

    # Benchmarks are added first so the portfolio line is drawn on top of them;
    # legendrank keeps the legend in the original order (Portfolio first).

    # 2. Market Benchmark (Russell 2000)
    if bench_vals and len(years) == len(bench_vals):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=years,
            y=bench_vals,
            name=names['benchmark'],
            mode=mode,
            line=dict(color='#ff7f0e', width=2, dash='dash'),
            marker=dict(symbol='square', size=4),
            opacity=0.8,
            legendrank=2,
            hovertemplate=HOVER_TEMPLATE
        ))

    # 3. Style Benchmark: Value Index
    if val_vals and len(years) == len(val_vals):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=years,
            y=val_vals,
            name=names['value'],
            mode=mode,
            line=dict(color='#2ca02c', width=1.5, dash='dot'),
            marker=dict(symbol='triangle-up', size=4),
            opacity=0.6,
            legendrank=3,
            hovertemplate=HOVER_TEMPLATE
        ))

    # 4. Style Benchmark: Growth Index
    if gro_vals and len(years) == len(gro_vals):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=years,
            y=gro_vals,
            name=names['growth'],
            mode=mode,
            line=dict(color='#d62728', width=1.5, dash='dot'),
            marker=dict(symbol='diamond', size=4),
            opacity=0.6,
            legendrank=4,
            hovertemplate=HOVER_TEMPLATE
        ))

    # 1. Primary Portfolio Strategy
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=years,
        y=port_vals,
        name='Portfolio',
        mode=mode,
        line=dict(color='#1f77b4', width=2.5),
        marker=dict(symbol='circle', size=6),
        legendrank=1,
        hovertemplate=HOVER_TEMPLATE
    ))

    # Title and Label Configuration
    if factor_names:
        clean_names = [name.replace('_', ' ').title() for name in factor_names]
        title_str = f'Cumulative Wealth: {", ".join(clean_names)}'
    else:
        title_str = 'Portfolio Growth Comparison'

    fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(text=f'<b>{title_str}</b>', font=dict(size=14)),
        height=500,
        hovermode='x unified',
        # Legend in the upper left, inside the plot area
        legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor='left', yanchor='top')
    )

    # Financial Axis Formatting
    fig.update_yaxes(
        title=dict(text='Portfolio Value (USD)', font=dict(size=12)),
        tickprefix='$',
        tickformat=',.0f',
        showgrid=True,
        griddash='dash'
    )

    if dates:
        return date_axis(fig, font_size=12)

    # Ensure X-axis utilizes integer year ticks
    fig.update_xaxes(
        title=dict(text='Year', font=dict(size=12)),
        tickformat='d',
        hoverformat='d',
        dtick=1,
        showgrid=True,
        griddash='dash'
    )

    return fig

def plot_top_bottom_percent(
    years: List[int],
    percent: float = 10.0,
    show_bottom: bool = True,
    benchmark_returns: Optional[List[float]] = None,
    growth_returns: Optional[List[float]] = None,
    value_returns: Optional[List[float]] = None,
    benchmark_label: str = 'Russell 2000',
    initial_investment: float = 1000000.0,
    baseline_portfolio_values: Optional[List[float]] = None,
    precomputed_top: Optional[Union[Dict[str, Any], List[float]]] = None,
    precomputed_bot: Optional[Union[Dict[str, Any], List[float]]] = None,
    growth_label: str = 'Growth Index',
    value_label: str = 'Value Index',
    dates: bool = False
) -> go.Figure:
    """
    Constructs a wealth-index chart comparing performance of top and bottom cohorts.

    WRDS runs pass their ETFs' labels, and dates=True when `years` are dates.

    Returns:
        go.Figure: The generated Plotly figure object.
    """
    fig = go.Figure()
    mode = line_mode(len(years))

    def _get_trajectory(series: Optional[List[float]]) -> Optional[List[float]]:
        if series is None:
            return None

        if len(series) == 0:
            return None

        # If the series already looks like wealth levels (same length as years
        # and starts at the initial investment), plot it directly.
        if (
            len(series) == len(years)
            and abs(float(series[0]) - float(initial_investment)) <= max(1.0, 0.001 * float(initial_investment))
        ):
            return series[:len(years)]

        vals = [initial_investment]
        for ret in series:
            multiplier = (ret / 100.0) if abs(ret) > 1.0 else ret
            vals.append(vals[-1] * (1 + multiplier))
        return vals[:len(years)]

    # 1. Index Trajectories (Benchmark, Growth, Value)
    indices = [
        (benchmark_returns, benchmark_label, '#d62728', 'dash', 'x'),
        (growth_returns, growth_label, '#ff7f0e', 'dot', 'diamond'),
        (value_returns, value_label, '#17becf', 'dot', 'square')
    ]

    for rets, label, color, style, marker in indices:
        vals = _get_trajectory(rets)
        if vals and len(vals) == len(years):
            fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
                x=years, y=vals, name=label,
                mode=mode,
                line=dict(color=color, dash=style, width=1.2),
                marker=dict(symbol=marker, size=3),
                opacity=0.6, hovertemplate=HOVER_TEMPLATE
            ))

    # 2. Bottom Cohort (Lower Visual Weight)
    if show_bottom and precomputed_bot is not None:
        bot_vals = precomputed_bot.get('portfolio_values', [initial_investment]) if isinstance(precomputed_bot, dict) else precomputed_bot
        if len(bot_vals) >= len(years):
            fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
                x=years, y=bot_vals[:len(years)], name=f'Bottom {percent}%',
                mode=mode,
                line=dict(color='#9467bd', width=1.5),
                marker=dict(symbol='triangle-down', size=4),
                opacity=0.6, hovertemplate=HOVER_TEMPLATE
            ))

    # 3. Top Cohort (High Contrast)
    if precomputed_top is not None:
        top_vals = precomputed_top.get('portfolio_values', [initial_investment]) if isinstance(precomputed_top, dict) else precomputed_top
        if len(top_vals) >= len(years):
            fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
                x=years, y=top_vals[:len(years)], name=f'Top {percent}%',
                mode=mode,
                line=dict(color='#2ca02c', width=2.0),
                marker=dict(symbol='triangle-up', size=5),
                hovertemplate=HOVER_TEMPLATE
            ))

    # 4. Active Portfolio Strategy
    if baseline_portfolio_values:
        common_len = min(len(years), len(baseline_portfolio_values))
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=years[:common_len], y=baseline_portfolio_values[:common_len],
            name='Active Strategy',
            mode=mode,
            line=dict(color='#003366', width=2.5),
            marker=dict(symbol='circle', size=4),
            hovertemplate=HOVER_TEMPLATE
        ))

    # Institutional Chart Formatting
    fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(text=f'<b>Factor Efficacy: Top vs. Bottom {percent}% Cohort Spread</b>',
                   font=dict(size=14)),
        height=500,
        hovermode='x unified',
        # Legend in the upper left, inside the plot area
        legend=dict(x=0.01, y=0.99, xanchor='left', yanchor='top', font=dict(size=10))
    )

    fig.update_yaxes(
        title=dict(text='Account Value (USD)', font=dict(size=11)),
        tickprefix='$',
        tickformat=',.0f',
        showgrid=True,
        griddash='dash'
    )
    if dates:
        date_axis(fig, font_size=11)
    else:
        fig.update_xaxes(
            title=dict(text='Year', font=dict(size=11)),
            tickformat='d',
            hoverformat='d',
            dtick=1,
            showgrid=True,
            griddash='dash'
        )

    fig.add_hline(y=initial_investment, line_color='#000000', line_dash='solid',
                  line_width=0.8, opacity=0.2)

    return fig

def merge_entries(*lists: Optional[Iterable[Dict[str, Any]]],
                  limit: int = MAX_BROWSER_ENTRIES) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Analyses from several lists, one per ID (the most recently saved), newest first,
    at most `limit`. Entries without an analysis ID (runs computed in the app) are left out.
    """
    by_id: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]] = {}
    for entries in lists:
        for entry in entries or []:
            analysis_id = (entry or {}).get('analysis_id')
            if not analysis_id:
                continue
            old = by_id.get(analysis_id)
            if old is None or (entry.get('saved_at') or '') > (old.get('saved_at') or ''):
                by_id[analysis_id] = dict(entry)
    return sorted(by_id.values(), key=lambda e: e.get('saved_at') or '', reverse=True)[:limit]

def sync_browser_analyses(session_entries: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> Optional[List[Dict[str, Any]]]:
    """
    Adds this session's analyses to the browser's list and returns that list (None until
    the browser has reported it once). Call on every run so new analyses are saved.
    """
    result = _browser_store()(
        data={'storage_key': BROWSER_STORAGE_KEY, 'max_entries': MAX_BROWSER_ENTRIES,
              'add': [e for e in session_entries if e.get('analysis_id')]},
        key='factor_lake_analysis_store',
        on_stored_change=lambda: None,
    )
    stored = getattr(result, 'stored', None)
    if stored is not None:
        st.session_state[BROWSER_ANALYSES_KEY] = stored
    return st.session_state.get(BROWSER_ANALYSES_KEY)

def build_holdings_display_table(rows: List[Dict[str, Any]], factor_headers: List[str]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Turns one year's holdings rows (from the backtest) into the table shown on
    screen and exported.

    Number columns are converted to numbers but kept at full precision; they
    are rounded on screen only (see holdings_number_formats).
    """
    holdings_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    for col in NUMBER_COLUMNS + list(factor_headers):
        if col in holdings_df.columns:
            holdings_df[col] = pd.to_numeric(holdings_df[col], errors='coerce')
    if 'Delisted' in holdings_df.columns:
        holdings_df['Delisted'] = holdings_df['Delisted'].astype(bool)
    return holdings_df

def holdings_period_return(results: Dict[str, Any], year: int) -> Optional[float]:
    """
    The backtest's portfolio return (in percent) for the period that starts at
    rebalance year `year`, or None when that year has no return.

    holdings_by_year holds the rebalance years in the same order as
    yearly_returns, so the year's position gives its return.
    """
    years = list(results.get('holdings_by_year') or {})
    returns = results.get('yearly_returns') or []
    if year not in years or years.index(year) >= len(returns):
        return None
    return returns[years.index(year)]

def build_run_label(run_id: int, factor_labels: List[str]) -> str:
    """
    Builds the tab label for a saved run, e.g. "Run 3: ROA % +1".

    The run id keeps labels unique, which the stateful Results tabs need.
    """
    if not factor_labels:
        return f"Run {run_id}"
    label = f"Run {run_id}: {factor_labels[0]}"
    if len(factor_labels) > 1:
        label += f" +{len(factor_labels) - 1}"
    return label

def main():
    """
    Orchestrates the primary application flow, including security authentication,
    parameter configuration, and multi-tab rendering.
    """
    # PASSWORD AUTHENTICATION (disabled for open access)
    # To re-enable: uncomment below and keep password in secrets/env
    # if not utils.check_password(st.secrets):
    #     st.stop()

    st.markdown(
        '<div class="main-header-container">' +
        '<div class="main-header">Factor-Lake Portfolio Analysis</div>' +
        '<a href="https://cornell-sysen-5900.github.io/Factor-Lake/" target="_blank" class="docs-icon-link" title="View Documentation">📚</a>' +
        '</div>',
        unsafe_allow_html=True
    )

    # Render Global Sidebar and capture configuration
    user_settings = sidebar.render_sidebar(config.SECTOR_OPTIONS, utils.describe_data_source(),
                                           utils.get_backtest_lambda_name(),
                                           on_data_mode_change=reset_factor_selection)
    use_lambda = utils.lambda_backtests_enabled(user_settings)
    # Legacy settings have no data_mode key
    data_mode = user_settings.get('data_mode', 'legacy')

    # A finished run opens the Results tab. The active tab can only be set
    # before st.tabs is drawn, so the run requests it and reruns (see below).
    if RUN_COMPLETE_KEY in st.session_state and st.session_state.get(MAIN_TABS_KEY) != "Results":
        _open_main_tab("Results")

    # Define primary application layout. Only the open tab is rendered.
    main_tabs = st.tabs(MAIN_TABS, key=_main_tabs_widget_key(), on_change=_on_main_tab_change)
    tab_analysis, tab_results, tab_viewer, tab_about = main_tabs
    st.session_state[MAIN_TABS_KEY] = next(label for tab, label in zip(main_tabs, MAIN_TABS) if tab.open)

    if tab_analysis.open:
        with tab_analysis:
            st.button(
                "Clear Parameters", key="clear_parameters", on_click=_clear_parameters,
                help="Remove selected factors and restore analysis settings to their defaults. "
                     "Saved results and cached source data are kept.",
            )
            if st.session_state.pop(PARAMETERS_CLEARED_KEY, False):
                # WRDS runs always go to Lambda, without Load Market Data
                next_step = ("Choose new inputs, then run the analysis." if use_lambda or data_mode == 'wrds' else
                             "Choose new inputs, then click Load Market Data and Run Portfolio Analysis.")
                st.info(f"Parameters cleared. {next_step} Your saved results are kept.")

            # Configuration phase: Capture factors and directions
            selected_factor_names, factor_directions = render_factor_selection(data_mode)

            if data_mode == 'wrds':
                _render_wrds_run(user_settings, selected_factor_names, factor_directions)
            else:
                _render_legacy_run(user_settings, use_lambda, selected_factor_names, factor_directions)

    if tab_results.open:
        with tab_results:
            # Performance Visualization phase
            if RUN_COMPLETE_KEY in st.session_state:
                st.success(st.session_state.pop(RUN_COMPLETE_KEY))
            if OPENED_MESSAGE_KEY in st.session_state:
                st.success(st.session_state.pop(OPENED_MESSAGE_KEY))
            # Open a saved analysis by its ID (it becomes the newest run tab), and this session's history
            render_open_saved_analysis(has_runs=bool(st.session_state.get('saved_runs')))
            history = st.session_state.get('analysis_history', [])
            render_analysis_history(history)
            render_earlier_analyses(earlier_analyses(st.session_state.get(BROWSER_ANALYSES_KEY), history))
            render_all_saved_analyses()
            if st.session_state.get('saved_runs'):
                render_saved_runs(st.session_state.saved_runs)
            else:
                st.info("Performance metrics will appear here after a successful analysis run.")

    if tab_viewer.open:
        with tab_viewer:
            # Raw data inspection and CSV export (reuses the data loaded in Analysis)
            if data_mode == 'wrds':
                st.caption(":material/info: The Data Viewer shows the Legacy data, not WRDS: switch the data "
                           "source to Legacy and click Load Market Data to use it.")
            render_data_viewer_tab()

    if tab_about.open:
        with tab_about:
            # Documentation phase
            render_about_tab()

    # Keep this session's analysis IDs in the browser too, so they can be found in later sessions
    sync_browser_analyses(st.session_state.get('analysis_history', []))

def initialize_environment() -> None:
    """
    Configures the system path and environment variables.

    Ensures the project root is accessible to the Python interpreter and 
    loads local environment variables if a .env file is present.
    """
    current_dir = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    project_root = current_dir.parent

    if str(project_root) not in sys.path:
        sys.path.insert(0, str(project_root))

    if not os.environ.get("STREAMLIT_RUNTIME_ENV"):
        env_path = project_root / '.env'
        if env_path.exists():
            with open(env_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
                for line in f:
                    line = line.strip()
                    if line and not line.startswith('#') and '=' in line:
                        key, value = line.split('=', 1)
                        os.environ.setdefault(key, value.strip("'\""))

def initialize_session_state() -> None:

    default_state = {

def get_data_source() -> str:
    """
    Picks where the market data is loaded from.

    FACTOR_LAKE_DATA_SOURCE ("s3" or "supabase") wins when it is set. Otherwise
    S3 is used whenever AWS credentials are configured, and Supabase is the fallback.
    """
    source = os.environ.get('FACTOR_LAKE_DATA_SOURCE', '').strip().lower()
    if source:
        if source not in DATA_SOURCES:
            raise ValueError(f"FACTOR_LAKE_DATA_SOURCE must be one of {DATA_SOURCES}, not '{source}'.")
        return source
    return 's3' if os.environ.get('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID') else 'supabase'

def load_shared_universe(source: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """
    Downloads the full universe once and shares it with every user session.

    Loading per session made each visitor wait for (and hold) a separate copy.
    A failed download raises and is not cached, so the next click retries.
    The returned frame is shared between sessions: copy it before modifying it.
    """
    from src.data_standardization import validate_universe
    if source == 's3':
        from src.s3_client import S3DataManager
        df = S3DataManager().fetch_all_data()
    else:
        from src.supabase_client import SupabaseManager
        df = SupabaseManager().fetch_all_data()
    validate_universe(df, source)
    return df

def load_and_process_data(user_settings: Dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """
    Orchestrates data fetching and universe filtering.

    Applies ESG restrictions, sector filters, and date constraints 
    to the raw dataset retrieved from the configured data source.

    raw_data is shared by every session (st.cache_resource), so it is never
    modified, and it is not copied whole: all filters form one row mask and only
    the kept rows are copied. When nothing is filtered out, rdata shares
    raw_data's columns, so treat rdata as read-only too.
    """
    from src.universe_selection import select_universe
    try:
        if st.session_state.raw_data is None:
            st.session_state.raw_data = load_shared_universe(get_data_source())

        # Year, sector and ESG fossil fuel filters (the backtest Lambda applies the same ones)
        df = select_universe(
            st.session_state.raw_data,
            int(user_settings['start_year']), int(user_settings['end_year']),
            selected_sectors=user_settings.get('selected_sectors'),
            restrict_fossil_fuels=bool(user_settings.get('restrict_fossil_fuels')),
        )

        st.session_state.rdata = df
        st.session_state.loaded_filters = _universe_filters(user_settings)
        st.session_state.data_loaded = True
        st.success(f"Universe Refined: {len(df):,} records prepared.")
    except Exception as e:
        st.error(f"Data Orchestration Error: {str(e)}")

def describe_compute(info: Optional[Dict[str, Any]]) -> str:
    """One line on where a result came from, e.g. "computed in AWS Lambda in 8.2 s"."""
    if not info:
        return "computed in this app"
    if info.get('opened'):
        text = "opened from a saved analysis"
        if info.get('computed_at'):
            text += f" (first computed {info['computed_at'].replace('T', ' ').rstrip('Z')} UTC)"
        return text
    if info.get('cached'):
        text = f"returned from the AWS Lambda result cache in {info['round_trip_seconds']:.1f} s"
        if info.get('computed_at'):
            text += f" (first computed {info['computed_at'].replace('T', ' ').rstrip('Z')} UTC)"
    else:
        text = (f"computed in AWS Lambda in {info['round_trip_seconds']:.1f} s "
                f"(backtest {info.get('compute_seconds') or 0:.1f} s)")
    if info.get('delivery') == 's3_link':
        text += ", downloaded from an S3 link"
    return text

def run_cohort(run: Dict[str, Any], cohort_pct: float):
    """
    Top vs bottom cohort portfolio values for a saved run, computed where the run
    was: in Lambda for Lambda runs (run['data'] is None), else locally on the run's data.

    Returns:
        (top values, bottom values, compute info or None for local runs)
    """
    from src.backtest_engine import run_cohort_comparison
    if run.get('data_mode') == 'wrds':
        result, info = _run_wrds_job(run, 'cohort', cohort_pct=cohort_pct)
        return result['top'], result['bottom'], info
    if run.get('data') is not None:
        top, bottom = run_cohort_comparison(
            data=run['data'],
            selected_factors=run['factors'],
            factor_directions=run['factor_directions'],
            cohort_pct=cohort_pct,
            user_settings=run['settings'],
        )
        return list(top), list(bottom), None

    from src.backtest_jobs import build_job
    function_name = run['compute'].get('function_name') or get_backtest_lambda_name()
    if not function_name:
        raise RuntimeError("Cohort comparisons for an opened analysis run in AWS Lambda, "
                           f"and no Lambda is configured ({BACKTEST_LAMBDA_ENV}).")
    job = build_job('cohort', run['factors'], run['factor_directions'], run['settings'],
                    factor_labels=dict(zip(run['factors'], run['factor_labels'])), cohort_pct=cohort_pct)
    result, info = get_lambda_client(function_name).run(job)
    return result['top'], result['bottom'], info

With Lambda backtests on (lambda_backtests_enabled), the inputs are sent to the backtest Lambda instead, which reads the data from S3; the run then keeps no data (run['data'] is None) and run['compute'] says how the Lambda produced the result.

def run_backtest_logic(user_settings: Dict[str, Any], 
                       factor_names: List[str], 
                       factor_dirs: Dict[str, str]) -> Optional[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Executes the portfolio backtesting engine and saves the run.

    Translates UI-friendly labels to internal database columns, runs the
    backtest, and saves a snapshot of the run (results plus the factors,
    directions, settings and data it used) as the newest entry in
    st.session_state.saved_runs.

    With Lambda backtests on (lambda_backtests_enabled), the inputs are sent to the
    backtest Lambda instead, which reads the data from S3; the run then keeps no data
    (run['data'] is None) and run['compute'] says how the Lambda produced the result.

    Returns:
        The saved run, or None if the run was rejected or failed (nothing is saved).
    """
    from src.backtest_engine import rebalance_portfolio
    from src.backtest_jobs import build_job
    from app.streamlit_config import FACTOR_METADATA, MAX_SAVED_RUNS
    from app.saved_runs import add_saved_run, build_run_label

    factor_labels = [f for f in factor_names if f in FACTOR_METADATA]
    if not factor_labels:
        st.warning("Select at least one factor before running the analysis.")
        return None
    if float(user_settings['initial_aum']) <= 0:
        st.warning("Initial AUM must be greater than $0.")
        return None

    try:
        # Mapping UI labels to internal SQL columns
        internal_factor_cols = [FACTOR_METADATA[f]['column'] for f in factor_labels]
        internal_directions = {
            FACTOR_METADATA[f]['column']: factor_dirs.get(f, 'top')
            for f in factor_labels
        }
        column_labels = {FACTOR_METADATA[f]['column']: f for f in factor_labels}

        if lambda_backtests_enabled(user_settings):
            # AWS Lambda reads the data from S3, filters it like Load Market Data and runs the same engine
            job = build_job('backtest', internal_factor_cols, internal_directions, user_settings,
                            factor_labels=column_labels)
            results, compute = get_lambda_client(get_backtest_lambda_name()).run(job)
            data, universe = None, _universe_filters(user_settings)
        else:
            data, compute = st.session_state.rdata, None
            universe = dict(st.session_state.get('loaded_filters') or {})
            # Portfolio simulation execution
            results = rebalance_portfolio(
                data,
                internal_factor_cols,
                factor_directions=internal_directions,
                start_year=int(user_settings['start_year']),
                end_year=int(user_settings['end_year']),
                initial_aum=user_settings['initial_aum'],
                benchmark_index=user_settings.get('benchmark_index', 1),
                top_pct=user_settings.get('top_pct', 10.0),
                use_market_cap_weight=user_settings.get('use_market_cap_weight', False),
                delisting_strategy=user_settings.get('delisting_strategy', 'zero_return'),
                factor_combination=user_settings.get('factor_combination', 'mixing'),
                factor_labels=column_labels
            )
    except Exception as e:
        st.error(f"Backtest Execution Error: {str(e)}")
        return None

    if not results.get('yearly_returns'):
        st.warning(
            "The backtest produced no yearly returns. "
            "Choose an End Year after the Start Year and check the loaded data covers that period."
        )
        return None

    # Save a snapshot so later sidebar/factor changes never alter this run
    run_id = st.session_state.next_run_id
    run = {
        'id': run_id,
        'label': build_run_label(run_id, factor_labels),
        'factor_labels': factor_labels,
        'factors': internal_factor_cols,
        'factor_directions': internal_directions,
        'settings': dict(user_settings),
        'universe': universe,
        'data': data,
        'results': results,
        'compute': compute,
        'cohort': None,
    }
    st.session_state.next_run_id = run_id + 1
    st.session_state.saved_runs = add_saved_run(
        st.session_state.saved_runs, run, MAX_SAVED_RUNS
    )
    add_to_history(run)
    return run

def run_wrds_backtest_logic(user_settings: Dict[str, Any], factor_names: List[str],
                            factor_dirs: Dict[str, str]) -> Optional[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Sends a WRDS backtest to the backtest Lambda and saves the run like a Legacy Lambda
    run (run['data'] is None), with data_mode 'wrds'.

    Returns:
        The saved run, or None if the run was rejected or failed (nothing is saved).
    """
    from src.wrds_jobs import build_wrds_job
    from app.streamlit_config import MAX_SAVED_RUNS, WRDS_FACTOR_METADATA
    from app.saved_runs import add_saved_run

    factor_labels = [f for f in factor_names if f in WRDS_FACTOR_METADATA]
    if not factor_labels:
        st.warning("Select at least one factor before running the analysis.")
        return None
    if float(user_settings['initial_aum']) <= 0:
        st.warning("Initial AUM must be greater than $0.")
        return None

    columns = [WRDS_FACTOR_METADATA[f]['column'] for f in factor_labels]
    directions = {WRDS_FACTOR_METADATA[f]['column']: factor_dirs.get(f, 'top') for f in factor_labels}
    try:
        job = build_wrds_job('backtest', columns, directions, user_settings,
                             factor_labels={WRDS_FACTOR_METADATA[f]['column']: f for f in factor_labels})
        results, compute = get_lambda_client(get_backtest_lambda_name()).run(job)
    except Exception as e:
        st.error(f"Backtest Execution Error: {str(e)}")
        return None

    run_id = st.session_state.next_run_id
    run = {
        'id': run_id,
        'label': _wrds_run_label(run_id, factor_labels, job['frequency']),
        'data_mode': 'wrds',
        'factor_labels': factor_labels,
        'factors': columns,
        'factor_directions': directions,
        'settings': dict(user_settings),
        'universe': _universe_filters(user_settings),
        'data': None,
        'results': results,
        'compute': compute,
        'cohort': None,
    }
    st.session_state.next_run_id = run_id + 1
    st.session_state.saved_runs = add_saved_run(st.session_state.saved_runs, run, MAX_SAVED_RUNS)
    add_to_history(run)
    return run

def add_to_history(run: Dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """
    Records a run in this session's history (st.session_state.analysis_history). It
    lives only in the session, so it lists only this user's own runs, including ones
    no longer shown as Results tabs (only the last MAX_SAVED_RUNS are kept there).
    Entries with an ID are also kept in the browser (app/analysis_history.py). WRDS
    entries also have a summary (data source, frequency, factors), as in the list of
    all saved analyses, because their label only names the frequency.
    """
    from datetime import datetime, timezone
    compute = run.get('compute') or {}
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    entry = {
        'label': run['label'],
        'analysis_id': compute.get('hash'),
        'how': 'opened' if compute.get('opened') else 'computed in Lambda' if compute else 'computed in this app',
        'time': now.strftime('%H:%M:%S UTC'),
        'saved_at': now.strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ'),
    }
    if run.get('data_mode') == 'wrds':
        from src.wrds_jobs import build_wrds_job
        from src.wrds_service import summarize_wrds_job
        entry['summary'] = summarize_wrds_job(build_wrds_job(
            'backtest', run['factors'], run['factor_directions'], run['settings'],
            factor_labels=dict(zip(run['factors'], run['factor_labels']))))
    st.session_state.analysis_history = st.session_state.get('analysis_history', []) + [entry]
